Google has yet to describe how its upcoming operating system will work and whether it can truly make more Android apps work better natively on a larger display. If that were it, then Googlebooks would just be another run-of-the-mill laptop being slowly squeezed by the RAM shortage. But MacObserver has shared a few more details about “Googlebook OS,” which seems to be the modern name for what was previously codenamed Aluminum OS. If you already guessed it has something to do with AI, congratulations. Documentation suggests you’ll be able to access Gemini for “personal proactive help,” likely in the form of cross-app actions like writing your emails or adding calendar events for you. Google is certainly going to fill these laptops to the brim with AI. An APK teardown by Android Authority earlier this month suggested that the laptops could use AI to automatically create “Collections” of your loose files sitting in your downloads folder and desktop. It could prove an actually useful feature if you have never learned any skills at file management. Surprisingly, the Lenovo leaks also mention a “Google facial authentication” that could be face unlock functionality, almost like Windows Hello’s facial unlock. There’s also a fingerprint reader for further biometric access. These Googlebooks also sport a special “G” key in place of the Windows button you find on most PCs’ keyboards. This key is likely how Google expects you to access these AI functions. And if you wanted to know what that “Glowbar” was for on these upcoming laptops, it’s supposed to indicate your laptop’s battery and charging levels. Most surprising of all, Google and its partner OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) seem like they will launch dedicated accessories for Googlebooks, including a “Lenovo AI Mouse” with an RGB light strip around the back. We expect the mouse may sync with the laptop’s Glowbar, but for how it will actually incorporate AI, we can expect it may interact with Google’s AI-ified mouse cursor. We’ll have to wait to see how many of these AI features actually run fully on-device and whether any of them prove useful. At the very least, the number of leaks indicates we won’t have to wait long.

item.title: This ‘Cell Tower in the Sky’ Just Completed a Record-Breaking 18,641-Mile Round Trip to Japan
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.79
An oblong silver airship recently completed a 30-day journey, flying through Earth’s stratosphere to deliver mobile broadband connectivity to cellphones. Aerospace company Sceye launched its Service Test 1 (ST1) mission on August 9 for a trans-Pacific flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. The airship operated for a week over Japan to test its capability to provide high-speed connectivity from the stratosphere for emergency and disaster response scenarios. “This mission proved not only that our technology, vehicle systems, payload, and operational infrastructure are ready for connectivity services, but also that the stratosphere is where the future non-terrestrial infrastructure lies,” Mikkel Vestergaard Frandsen, Founder and CEO of Sceye, said in a statement. “The stratosphere is what will enable the always-on future—including the promised land of 6G.” Going up Sceye’s experimental vehicles, officially called High Altitude Platform Systems, are designed to operate like cell towers in the sky. Their balloon-like design allows them to stay suspended in the stratosphere for months or years at a time. The airship relies on the buoyancy of helium to stay airborne instead of consuming fuel or electrical energy. Meanwhile, solar cells placed on top of the airship’s hull power its communications payload and help it maintain its position against stratospheric winds. During its latest test flight, Sceye’s ST1 traveled 18,641 miles (30,000 kilometers) before arriving at the airspace near Sceye’s headquarters in Moriarty, New Mexico, on September 5. The vehicle completed additional testing before a planned termination and descent. Testing, testing ST1 carried SceyeCell, an airborne cellular network antenna designed to deliver wide-area mobile broadband directly to standard devices from the stratosphere. When deployed at full scale, a single airship could cover the equivalent area of approximately 500 terrestrial towers, according to Sceye. During the flight, the airship demonstrated mobile broadband communications, including text messaging, voice calls, internet access, and video streaming. The platform also tested emergency calls using an emergency alert messaging system designed for large-scale disasters, as well as communications with drones. With SceyeCell, the company is aiming to compete with satellites delivering connectivity from low-Earth orbit without the operational cost of being in space. The stratosphere, according to Sceye, is close enough to Earth for high-capacity connectivity and observation while at a high-enough altitude to offer a wide-area reach. Sceye’s vehicles operate similar to a geostationary satellite, except 1,800 times closer to Earth, according to the company. “Together ground, stratosphere, and space – each operating at their optimal strengths, will change the course of humanity,” Frandsen said.

item.title: Never Forget, AI Slop Is Polluting 9/11 History on the Internet as We Speak
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.55
became known as the Man in the Red Bandana after stories spread about his heroism on September 11, 2001. Now, an AI-generated image purporting to show Crowther rescuing people from the World Trade Center is going viral—the latest example of how fabricated images could distort our collective memory of 9/11 for generations. The 24-year-old Crowther was working on the 104th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center when a plane struck on that fateful day. Crowther, an equities trader, was also a volunteer firefighter and is credited with helping save the lives of at least a dozen people. He reportedly helped guide people to the lone functioning stairwell and even carried some people down the stairs himself. He died when the South Tower collapsed. President Donald Trump awarded Crowther the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday and, as always, the president had to make it about himself, insisting he doesn’t like that the man in the red bandana had become much more famous than him. Trump on a deceased 9/11 rescuer: “The Man in the Red Bandana. Have you heard of him? He’s become more famous than me. I don’t like it. Very unhappy. But he’s become much more famous than me.” — FactPost (@factpostnews.bsky.social) September 8, 2026 at 8:25 AM Crowther’s story of heroism is very real according to multiple witnesses, but the image that’s going viral of Crowther isn’t. There are no known photos of Crowther in action on September 11th. One major problem with the proliferation of AI images is that AI image detectors can be unreliable. Gizmodo ran the image above through ChatGPT and asked if it was created with AI. The response from ChatGPT: “It very likely is not AI-generated. It appears to be a genuine historical photograph rather than an AI-created image.” The explanation from ChatGPT went on to insist that the image has features “you’d expect from a real news photograph” and that it’s “consistent with photographs taken during the evacuation of the World Trade Center after the September 11 attacks.” When Gizmodo uploaded the image to Grok, the chatbot claimed that it was “a well-known photograph from the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks,” but when pressed on whether it was authentic, Grok finally admitted it might be fake. Claude said the image was a photo but likely a dramatization and not created with AI. When I asked Claude to do a reverse image search, the chatbot said it “confirmed” the image was from a documentary or similar that depicted the events and wasn’t made with AI: “So to directly answer your question: no, this doesn’t look AI-generated — it’s a reenactment/dramatization photo…” The definitive documentary on Crowther, Man In Red Bandana (2017), does feature an actor very briefly recreating some of his actions while saving people, but it doesn’t match up with the AI image that’s currently going viral. The actor playing Crowther in that documentary is wearing a white t-shirt, not a button-up shirt and tie. When we tried Gemini and asked if the image had the SynthID watermark, which is added to all images created with Google’s AI tools, the chatbot said that it couldn’t check that. Google opened up SynthID detection to all Gemini users last year, so that was a weird claim. After being pressed, the chatbot said we were right that this feature had been added and Gemini hadn’t found it to have SynthID. The hallucination and initial refusal to check should definitely give us pause when relying on the safeguards AI companies have supposedly created for us to fact-check our own reality. In a somewhat odd twist, Google’s AI overview insists the image is a “dramatic scene from the 1999 disaster television miniseries Aftershock: Earthquake in New York,” something that’s both untrue and would date the image to before the terror attacks of 2001. The image is not genuine and was definitely made with AI. Anyone can tell that just by looking at it, to say nothing of the fact that reverse image searches reveal it was likely never published before this week. Other AI images of Crowther have also popped up this year, like the one below from Facebook. Roughly 25% of Americans alive in 2026 weren’t born yet on September 11, 2001. The images that live on and spread online shape how we understand that day. And there are plenty of other AI images circulating online that purport to show what happened that day. Even when the underlying events are grounded in reality, fake images distort how we understand history. In some ways, this isn’t exactly a new problem. Here at Gizmodo, we spent much of the 2010s debunking fake historical images that were created with Photoshop-style tools. But there was a built-in friction with old-school Photoshop. Users were required to have some degree of talent and spend a bit of time creating fakes. These days, anyone can prompt a fake image using nothing but words and output a photo-realistic result in seconds. That low barrier to entry has created an environment where we often refuse to believe things that are real because they could be AI. People like Donald Trump even exploit this, insisting that authentic photos and videos must be AI because they’re inconvenient to his narrative. There have been a lot of those instances, believe it or not. And we’re all much dumber for it. READ MORE:

item.title: 5 3D-printed clock projects you should make time for this weekend (Sep 11 - 13)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.51
I don’t currently have any visible clocks on display in my house. I’m never without my watch or phone, and I decided that if I were to sacrifice some space for a dedicated timepiece, it would need to be something special, different, or interesting. That’s exactly what these 3D-printed clocks are. Fully functional mechanical 3D-printed clock Complete with pendulum You can buy a simple clock mechanism for relatively cheap; they’re even available for sale on the MakerWorld shop. Most of the clock designs featured today don’t actually make use of a simple mechanism, instead opting for more interesting ways to keep time. This mechanical clock is fully 3D printed except for one part: the pendulum rod. The designer recommends an “M6 threaded rod with a minimum length of 1.1 m" in order to keep the mechanism moving and the clock accurate. This design “costs” around 700g in filament and presents you with a detailed yet satisfying build project. Take a peek at the detailed instructions before you print it to see what’s entailed—it looks a lot like putting LEGO kits together to me. Once built, the clock should keep itself running and will almost certainly start a conversation with anyone who is visiting. This is the revised second version, but the original is still available (which requires more non-3D-printed parts). Word Clock Bring it to life with an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Zero W A word clock is, unsurprisingly, a clock that tells the time with words. Rather than seeing the numbers 10:20, you’ll see the words “twenty past ten” instead. This is a fun spin on the simple act of telling the time, bound to brighten up any kitchen, office, or anywhere else you want to stick it. This 3D-printed word clock uses an addressable LED strip, a printer with a multi-material system (like Bambu Lab’s AMS), and a Raspberry Pi Zero W or ESP32 microcontroller. Some soldering is required, and you’ll need a few extra bits like screws and wires (on top of 2m of LED strip). Flip clock With an RTC module to track the time when it’s off An oldie but a goody, this flip clock design has been sitting on Thingiverse since 2020, with a GitHub repo dedicated to the build that includes a bill of materials, plus instructions for printing, assembling, and calibrating the clock. At the end of it, you’ll have a physical moving flip clock made from 3D-printed parts. Powered by a small Arduino-compatible microcontroller, the clock uses stepper motors and drivers to move the flaps. In addition to tracking time even when the power is off, the clock will automatically adhere to US daylight saving time. Wandering hour clock Once you figure out how it works, it’s great I spent a few minutes staring at this clock, trying to figure out how exactly one is supposed to read the time. It turns out that it’s incredibly easy: the current hour always points at a minute counter at the bottom of the screen. So as 9 o’clock approaches the 60-minute mark, 10 o’clock will reach the 0-minute mark and start again. A rework of an existing project, the wandering clock depends on an upcycled IKEA Bondis wall clock (though you could probably adapt other mechanisms to suit), a few screws, and some bearings. The Printables project has detailed instructions for assembling everything, and of course you can customize the colors to suit whatever room you’re putting it in. Cube clock Two cubes move to tell the time This minimalist cube clock works with Bambu Lab’s clock component kit or cheap IKEA (and other) clock mechanisms. It’s incredibly simple: the background is a static cube, while two more cubes sit on top. One is connected to the minute hand, the other to the hour hand. As the time changes, so does the shape of the clock, making for an interesting and ever-changing timepiece. There’s nothing particularly complex about this one, but it’s the perfect example of a fast project that you can make yourself using old clock mechanisms that might just be lying around. Go even further by customizing the clock face, changing the colors, or adding a light to the back of the design. Many of these projects depend on an ESP32 or similar microcontroller. Check out some more 3D printing projects you can only make with an ESP32.

item.title: 1 cell, 1 formula: 5 Excel functions that replace repetitive calculations
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.23
For longer than I care to remember, I've written Excel formulas, dragged them down hundreds of rows, copied calculations across columns, and built running totals one cell at a time. This works, but I always find I'm doing too much work, especially when some of those jobs can be handled by a single formula sitting in a single cell. If you've used Excel functions like FILTER, SORTBY, or UNIQUE, you'll be familiar with the idea of entering one formula and letting Excel return an entire result. The five functions below take a similar approach, but they work slightly differently: they let you define a calculation once and apply it repeatedly to an array, row, column, or sequence of values. MAP applies a calculation to corresponding values Apply the same logic repeatedly MAP takes one or more arrays, passes their corresponding values to a LAMBDA function, and returns the results as a separate array. This is ideal when you want to perform the same calculation across a set of values without repeating the formula on each row. The syntax is: =MAP( array1, [array2,...], LAMBDA(parameter1, [parameter2, ...], calculation) ) The first one or more arguments are the arrays you want to work with, and the LAMBDA defines what Excel should do with each set of corresponding values. In my T_Sales table, I want to calculate the discounted sale value for every transaction and then classify each one as either "High" or "Standard" depending on whether the result exceeds $1,000. To do that, in cell G2, I'll write: =MAP( T_Sales[Units], T_Sales[Price], T_Sales[Discount], LAMBDA(u, p, d, LET(value, u*p*(1-d), IF(value>1000, "High", "Standard"))) ) MAP takes the three columns as separate arrays. Then, for each row, the LAMBDA receives the units, price, and discount, calculates the discounted value, and returns the classification. Yes, I could do this by repeating a formula down a calculated column, but with MAP, I only need to define the multistep logic once. It also means I don't have to worry about accidentally overwriting one of the calculations. BYROW gives the LAMBDA an entire row Process one row at a time BYROW takes an array and passes each row to a LAMBDA function separately. Rather than working with individual values, the LAMBDA receives the entire row, which means you can perform calculations or tests across all the values in that row. Here's the syntax: =BYROW( array, LAMBDA(row, calculation) ) The key difference from MAP is that BYROW gives the LAMBDA the whole row, rather than individual values from several arrays. In my student-score dataset, I want to decide whether each student passes based on two conditions: their average score must be at least 80, and none of their individual scores can be below 70. So in G2, I'll enter: =BYROW( T_Scores[[Math]:[History]], LAMBDA(row, IF(AND(AVERAGE(row)>=80, MIN(row)>=70), "Pass", "Review")) ) For each row, BYROW passes the four subject scores into the LAMBDA as an array. AVERAGE checks the student's overall score, while MIN makes sure their lowest score is at least 70. The IF then returns either "Pass" or "Review" for each student. Again, I could achieve a similar outcome using a helper column. The difference is that BYROW lets me work with the entire row at once, so I can build one calculation around several values without maintaining a separate formula for every row. BYCOL applies one calculation to every column Process one column at a time BYCOL works much like BYROW, except it passes each column to the LAMBDA instead. This is useful when you want to perform the same calculation or test independently on every column in an array. Here's the function's structure: =BYCOL( array, LAMBDA(column, calculation) ) This time, my aim is to calculate the percentage of students who scored at least 80 in each subject. After applying the Percentage number format to cells B13:E13, I'll input this formula into cell B13: =BYCOL( T_Scores[[Math]:[History]], LAMBDA(column, COUNTIF(column, ">=80")/ROWS(column)) ) BYCOL passes each subject's scores to the LAMBDA. COUNTIF counts how many scores are 80 or higher, while ROWS provides the number of students, so the result returns a percentage for each subject. SCAN keeps every intermediate result Keep every step along the way There are several ways to create a running total in Excel, but SCAN is my go-to method nowadays. It applies a calculation sequentially to an array while retaining the result from each step, so it's ideal for calculations where each result depends on the previous one. The basic syntax is: =SCAN( [initial_value], array, LAMBDA(accumulator, value, calculation) ) initial_value establishes the starting point. The LAMBDA then receives the accumulated result so far and the next value in the array, then calculates the next result. In my T_Sales table, I'm looking to calculate a running total of units sold as I move down the sales records. To do that, in cell G2, I'll write: =SCAN( 0, T_Sales[Units], LAMBDA(total, units, total+units) ) The accumulator starts at zero. SCAN then adds the first number of units to it, carries that result into the next calculation, and continues down the array. The result is a spilled list of running totals: 3, 11, 26, 48, and so on, ending at 256. Instead of repeating a formula like =SUM($C$2:C2) down the column or adding each row to the previous result, SCAN carries the previous result into the next calculation, returning the entire running total from one formula in one cell. REDUCE keeps only the final result Accumulate values in the background REDUCE is closely related to SCAN, but it returns only the final accumulated result. It repeatedly applies a calculation to an array, carrying the result from one step into the next. Here's how it works: =REDUCE( [initial_value], array, LAMBDA(accumulator, value, calculation) ) Like SCAN, it starts with an initial value and passes an accumulator and the next value into the LAMBDA. The difference is that REDUCE returns the accumulator after the final value has been processed. Using my T_Inflation data, my aim is to calculate how a product's value changes over six years, starting with its original value and applying each year's inflation rate to the previous year's result. Here's the formula I'll need in cell B2: =REDUCE( B1, T_Inflation[Rate], LAMBDA(balance, inflation, balance*(1+inflation)) ) This is a situation where REDUCE makes more sense than simply adding the percentages together, because each year's calculation depends on the result of the previous one. Let one formula handle the repetition It's easy to fall back on the Excel methods you've been using for years, especially when you already know they'll get the job done. These LAMBDA helper functions take a little getting used to, but after you've used them a few times, they can save you from writing several formulas or repeating the same calculation across a worksheet. Instead, you can define the logic once and let a single formula handle the repetition for you.

item.title: I got DOOM running on Android Auto, and it's exactly as impractical as it sounds
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.96
“Can it run DOOM?” It’s the question people love to half-jokingly ask about every gadget with a screen. Android, of course, can run DOOM — but what about Android Auto? That’s an entirely different beast. At first thought, you might think it would be an easy and resounding, “Yes! Of course, Android Auto can run DOOM.” That is the correct answer, but it’s far from easy. Android Auto exists in a weird place between full-blown Android and a glorified monitor. Android Auto is Android, but also not It’s complicated The thing that makes Android Auto so useful is the fact that it’s literally the same Android that’s on your phone. Even if you didn’t already know this, you’re well aware of the benefits. It’s the reason why your phone apps are present, signed in, and ready to be picked up where you left off on the car screen. That being said, not all of your phone apps are available in the Android Auto interface. Developers need to build in-car compatibility into their apps, ensure they meet Google’s car app quality guidelines, and they must fit into a Google-approved driving category. Android Auto apps generally fall into five categories: navigation, media, communication, utilities, and “parked.” Apps in the first four categories can be used in some capacity while driving, but the “parked” category is for apps that can’t be used while the vehicle is in motion. This includes video players, browsers, and games. So, it’s obviously not as easy as toggling a switch to make an app suddenly work on an Android Auto screen. That’s why only a small fraction of the apps on your phone are available, and an even smaller selection of games. Plus, most games are simply too complicated to be worth playing on a small screen in your car while parked. But when did practicality stop anyone from putting DOOM on a strange device? DOOM can run on Android Auto If you’re willing to do the work As I said at the top, DOOM can indeed run on Android Auto. However, it’s not as simple as downloading the official mobile version of DOOM from the Play Store. Instead, we’ll need to take advantage of a clever GitHub project. DOOM Mobile is a cross-platform implementation of the classic 1993 game that works on Android, iPhone, Windows, and MacCatalyst. Unlike many other projects that utilize emulators and wrappers, this is a full C# port of the original engine. It runs fully natively on your phone, and that’s evidence of the fact that you need to own a real copy of DOOM to play. The game needs a DOOM data .wad file in order to play past a short demo. I’ll be the first to admit that most of the technical explanation is out of my wheelhouse. For those who are interested in the nitty-gritty, I’ll spit out some details. Game frames are rendered using hardware-accelerated SkiaSharp v3 integrated with DrawnUI for .NET MAUI. The wall and level calculations are computed in C#, but the final rendered game texture is passed through a shader to allow GPU-side visual processing. Controlling the game works with touch or keyboard controls, depending on your device. On a phone, you can swipe around to move and turn, tap to shoot, and simply select items from the HUD and on-screen menus. That’s how the game is controlled on an Android Auto screen. Now, here’s the big catch. You can’t download an APK from the project’s “Releases” tab. Instead, you’ll need to compile it yourself in Microsoft Visual Studio with the .NET Multi-platform App UI workload installed or JetBrains Rider. I have no experience with either of these, so I enlisted the help of a good friend. After I installed the APK on my phone, it appeared in the Android Auto launcher with all of the other apps. No hacks or developer options required. It opened and was playable with touch controls just like on my phone. Next time you’re stuck in traffic, you can pick off some monsters with your BFG. That’s one more for the list of devices that can play DOOM.

item.title: These 5 underrated smart home upgrades keep your lights working when the internet goes down
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.72
Smart bulbs are one of the most common entries into the world of smart home devices, but they're not without their problems. If your internet goes down, you may find that you lose features or simply can't control your bulbs at all. There are several ways to stop this from happening. Use Matter devices with local control Alexa doesn't always need the cloud Popular smart home ecosystems such as Alexa and Google Home have made many smart homes heavily reliant on the cloud. With a Works with Google Home light bulb, for example, when you ask your smart speaker to turn on the light, the spoken command is sent from your speaker to Google's cloud, which interprets the command and sends a message to the smart bulb manufacturer's cloud, which sends the appropriate command to the bulb to turn on. If the internet goes down, the whole thing falls apart. Matter changes this, because commands are designed to travel locally over Wi-Fi or Thread. Google states that when you're at home, commands to Matter devices are carried out locally without an internet connection. The same is true of Alexa. Alexa can communicate with Matter devices locally, allowing supported Alexa-enabled devices to control them even when the internet is down. With supported Echo devices, Alexa voice commands can also continue to work during an internet outage. Move lighting automations to Home Assistant Run your smart home completely locally If features. There is an alternative that can be set up to work completely locally. Home Assistant is free and open-source smart home software that you run on your own hardware. You can run it on anything from a Raspberry Pi or old laptop to a mini PC or NAS. Home Assistant is designed with local control and privacy as the focus. The beauty of Home Assistant is that it doesn't care what ecosystem your smart home products are designed to work with. You can add Alexa-compatible devices, Apple Home devices, and Google devices, and control them all just the same. You can even set up a local voice assistant that allows you to control your smart home with your voice, without the need for an internet connection. Switch from Wi-Fi to Zigbee bulbs Your lights don't need an internet connection Just because you're using Home Assistant, it doesn't automatically make your smart home entirely local. If you're using Wi-Fi smart bulbs that are controlled by a cloud service, then your smart home is still not fully local. Commands from Home Assistant still need to reach the cloud to control your lights. You can make your lighting fully local by using Zigbee smart bulbs so your bulbs can talk directly to your smart home over your local Zigbee network without needing to use the cloud. Even proprietary systems such as Philips Hue can be controlled locally by Home Assistant using Local Push. Some optional Hue features still rely on the cloud, but all the core features can work locally. You can also cut Philips Hue out of the loop completely and connect your Philips Hue bulbs directly to Home Assistant using an option such as Zigbee2MQTT. With a suitable Zigbee coordinator, Home Assistant can then control your smart bulbs directly, without the need for a Hue Bridge. Another benefit of Zigbee is that even if your router goes down, Home Assistant can continue to talk to your smart bulbs over the Zigbee network. Automations that control your lights can continue to run as long as they're not reliant on your local Wi-Fi network. Add Zigbee binding Keep your lights working even when your smart hub is unreachable Even though Zigbee smart bulbs can be controlled from Home Assistant without an internet connection or even a local Wi-Fi network, they still need something to send them commands. If your Home Assistant server is out of action, you won't be able to control your bulbs from your phone, from dashboards, or using smart buttons that send commands via Home Assistant. That's where Zigbee binding can help. It's possible to bind a Zigbee controller such as a remote or smart button directly to a specific Zigbee bulb. With the binding in place, the command is sent directly from the controller to the bulb over your Zigbee network, without needing to go through a smart home hub or Zigbee coordinator at all. With supported devices, even if your smart home hub has shut down or your Zigbee coordinator has come unplugged, the Zigbee button can talk directly to the Zigbee bulb and turn your lights on and off. Use smart switches with local control Dumb bulbs don't care if the internet is down With smart bulbs, the hardware required to communicate with other devices is inside the bulb itself. You can take this out of the bulbs' hands by installing smart switches and using them with standard dumb bulbs. Smart switches solve many of the problems with smart bulbs, including the fact that if you turn off the power to a smart bulb at the switch, you can't control it at all. With a smart switch, you can manually turn the power on and off at the switch while still controlling the switch itself through your smart home. If your internet goes down, or your smart home server stops working, you can continue to use a smart switch manually, although you may lose remote control. It's one of the best options for setting up lighting that continues to work how the rest of your household would expect. Your lights don't have to rely on the internet Cloud-based smart devices are very convenient, but convenience comes at a price. Not only can these devices stop working properly when the internet goes down, but smart home companies can even stop supporting cloud-based smart home devices altogether. That's why a fully local smart home can often be the better choice.

item.title: The one cheap smart home upgrade your router needs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.51
Occasionally rebooting your router and modem is pretty normal, and some routers even have a reboot schedule function that can take care of this for you. Though problematic network equipment should be replaced, adding a smart plug to your setup can save you effort and even automate the entire process. Buying the right smart plug It depends on your smart home platform Rebooting your router usually means cutting power for around 10 seconds, then firing it back up and waiting for everything to return to normal. While you can do this by physically walking to the router, being able to do so remotely is more convenient. To enable this functionality, you’ll need a smart plug. This can’t be just any smart plug, however. After all, smart plugs that depend on Wi-Fi will cease to function when the network goes down. Instead, you should pick a smart plug that uses a different type of wireless communication. Which you choose largely depends on what smart home platform you’re using. For Home Assistant users, the sky is the limit. As long as you add the necessary adapter to your setup—like a Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 for Thread or Zigbee and a ZWA-2 for Z-Wave—you’re set for as long as your server is up, and the plug has power. You can also use Bluetooth smart plugs to achieve the same outcome. Apple Home users can choose Matter over Thread devices, particularly since modern Apple hubs like the HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K operate as Thread border routers. The same is true for some models of Amazon Echo and Google Nest devices. Of course, you’ll also need to pair these devices with smart plugs that use the Thread protocol. Both Google and Amazon have been slow out of the gate to embrace local control of smart home technology, which is why I’d urge alternatives. Limitations to be aware of Another reason to pick a local solution like Home Assistant Keep in mind that when your router goes offline, so too will your primary means of communicating with your smart home dashboard. This is true of all smart home platforms, which means that although you’ll be able to turn your plug off manually, you won’t necessarily be able to switch it back on. Home Assistant users can get around this by building a script that restarts their router, tying basic on-off functionality to a Zigbee (or similar) remote, or building an automation that detects connectivity issues and restarts the router or modem. If you aren’t using Home Assistant, you’re pretty much out of luck when it comes to manual restarts, though there are some other options you can explore. Perform restarts manually No need to unplug anything If you want to reboot your router or modem manually using Home Assistant, head to Settings > Automations & scenes and click on “Scripts” at the top of the page. Now click “+ Create script” and add a Device action for the plug you want to switch off (or add two, if you have separate network equipment) to turn off. Add a delay, then turn your network equipment back on again. You can now add your script to a dashboard of your choosing, or run it using the Scripts menu any time you need it. Alternatively, you can use a remote and create an automation so that the remote either runs the script you’ve created (perhaps with a long press) or bind buttons accordingly so that they control your smart plugs. This bypasses the need to switch your plug on manually using your Home Assistant dashboard (which is inaccessible whenever your network goes down). Some brands of smart devices can be bound so that they do not need a hub. For example, IKEA's Tretakt plug can be bound to a Rodret remote by holding the pairing button down while within range until the light flashes. Schedule regular reboots It certainly can't hurt My TP-Link Archer AX72 modem includes a “Reboot schedule” that restarts the modem at a time of my choosing. I don’t use this, mostly because I’ve got a smart home to do the heavy lifting. My router is only around a year old, so I’m hoping to get a bit more life out of it before it starts routinely giving up the ghost. That said, there are some good arguments to be made for routinely restarting your router. If you find that your router routinely crashes, a weekly restart might be the remedy you need until you get around to replacing it. You can schedule this basic functionality with most smart home platforms. Home Assistant makes it easy with its advanced automations, but you can get around the limited automation possibilities in a platform like Apple Home by creating two automations (one to turn the plug off, another to turn it on, a minute apart) provided you’re using Thread and not Wi-Fi. Go one better and reboot automatically Automate it! By far the best solution is to only restart your router when you need to. You can use Home Assistant to monitor your home internet connection and only initiate a restart after a set period of no connectivity. Check out our full guide on how to do this. Amazon, Google, and Apple’s smart home platforms lack the ability to create these kinds of complex automations. Some smart plugs may connect to an ecosystem-dependent app that allows them to be programmed, but that’ll depend on exactly what you’ve got. If you’re looking for another solution, why not give the Keep Connect network equipment smart plug a whirl. It’s a purpose-built device that only cuts power to your network equipment when the internet connection goes down. Keep Connect Automatic Router Rebooter - Brand - Keep - Schedules - Yes This is not your typical smart plug. The Keep Connect Automatic Router Rebooter triggers a power cycle when it detects a connection loss to automatically reboot your devices without you having to lift a finger. Take the time to improve your home network Rebooting your router can solve all manner of network problems, but you should really look at replacing network equipment that is constantly letting you down. Check out our top picks for routers.

item.title: How I turned my Linux terminal sessions into daily speedrun challenges
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.36
I’ve been using Linux for many, many years now, but I still keep learning new things all the time. It seems like, no matter what task you’re running, there’s a faster way to do it. So I decided to start focusing on these speed gains to see just how fast my terminal life can be. Now that I’m measuring command times and identifying performance gains, my day-to-day Linux use is getting more and more efficient. Here’s how. Start timing your commands Identifying the time sinks is the first step to fixing them Of course, the easiest way to time a command is with the existing time command. You can use it to time a program, so it’s great if you’re trying to optimize a specific command or a script you’ve written. But using time as a simple, general-purpose reporting tool is awkward, and I wanted a quick way of discovering what I actually spend time using the terminal for. Using zsh, you can hook into two events: preexec, which runs just before the shell executes a command, and precmd, which runs just before it returns to the prompt. timer_preexec() { TIMER_START=$EPOCHREALTIME } timer_precmd() { if [ -n "$TIMER_START" ]; then local duration=$(( EPOCHREALTIME - TIMER_START )) # do something useful with $duration here unset TIMER_START fi } add-zsh-hook preexec timer_preexec add-zsh-hook precmd timer_precmd In the full version of this script, I set the PROMPT variable inside time_precmd if it exceeds a threshold, so I get notified whenever a command takes more than a certain time. This is just the beginning of this approach; you could go much further and keep a proper record if you choose. Another approach uses the REPORTTIME zsh environment variable to automatically run time with every command: export REPORTTIME=0 You can set REPORTTIME to a number of seconds to only report on commands that take longer. Speeding up your day-to-day terminal use There’s often a quicker way to do something The second part of speed running is using shortcuts to work faster. These may seem like small gains at first, but over time they will combine to form large savings and reduce everyday frustration. Stop using the Up arrow I waste a lot of time on the command line rerunning or rewriting previous commands. The history features of your shell make this very easy: press Up a number of times to find a previous command, then hit Enter to rerun it. Or use Left, Right, and Backspace to edit it, then run it. Maybe you’ve even progressed to Ctrl + A to jump to the beginning of the line. It turns out that most of this long-winded typing is unnecessary. For a start, there’s !$ which expands to the last argument of the previous command, letting you do things like this: mkdir -p my/new/directory cd !$ I find this comes in handy when running a command I’ve just made executable (although be sure to supply the ./ prefix if it’s not already in your PATH): chmod +x foo.sh ./!$ There’s a vast number of history expansion shortcuts, like !! which expands to the previous command: apt install something # oops, need to be root... sudo !! But these techniques are far from the only way you can rewrite past commands. Another approach—and probably my top recommendation—is caret substitution: $ cd my/new/directry cd: no such file or directory $ ^tr^tor cd my/new/directory Using this syntax, your shell will take the previous command, replace the first instance of the first string with the second, and rerun the result. I’m now forcing myself to adopt this technique instead of the manual up-arrow approach, and I’m pleasantly surprised by just how much faster it is, now that I’m used to thinking about the fix and how to make it. Finally, the fc command is probably the most useful one you’re not already using. By default, it opens the last command in your terminal editor, then runs it when you exit. If you want to make more significant changes to a command, it’s typically faster than caret substitution, history shortcuts, or manually moving the cursor. Use aliases and functions There are probably commands — and sets of commands — you run all the time without even thinking about it. You’re on autopilot, so the process is quick and easy, but it could be so much quicker. If you’re running a command in the same way, again and again, consider an alias. Aliases provide basic text replacement, so instead of typing ls -lh every time you want a long file listing, you can do this instead: ll To set that up, you’ll need to define an alias, probably in a file like .bashrc. Simply use the alias command, pick a short series of letters that aren’t already in use, and define the expanded command in full: alias ll='ls -lh' The gains might seem insignificant, but they’ll grow the longer your commands get. For example, I like to use eza instead of ls, so my alias looks like this: alias ll='eza --long --sort=size --reverse' That’s a lot of typing saved, especially since I use this alias many times over, every single day. If your aliases start getting more complicated, consider defining a simple function instead. Functions let you use parameters and control flow, and you can also call them from your own shell scripts. One of the most useful functions I always make sure to define is this one: mkd() { mkdir -p -- "$1" && cd -P -- "$1" || exit } For a start, notice how the name of this function is shorter than the standard mkdir; that's already a saving every time you create a directory! But, more importantly, it does the thing I usually do once I’ve created a directory anyway: entering that directory with cd. I also send the -p option to mkdir by default, since this creates any intermediate directories, like the docs in “mkd docs/finance.” It’s important to note that there are some minor drawbacks to using -p all the time: there are some types of errors that might pass you by, for example. But a true speed runner doesn’t concern themselves with these kinds of risks; they get everything right, as quickly as possible. Use faster tools Although the core Linux toolset is stable, mature, and reliable, alternatives are available. Many of these are written in more modern languages, like Rust, which is fast and safe. Better command-line tools include tmux, for session management, fzf and fd, fast alternatives to find/grep, and zoxide, which makes navigation much more efficient than cd. Know your limitations — and get rid of them! Your shell has many powerful features that not only let you measure your productivity, but also allow you to improve it. Tab completion, background processes, and command chaining are just a few of those I haven’t mentioned here.

item.title: 5 open-source desktop apps that I always recommend instead of their paid rivals
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.83
Any time I recommend software to a friend, there is always an inevitable question: How much does it cost? The quality isn't necessarily the discerning factor—no one wants to pay for something if it isn't necessary. That makes free, open-source tools very easy to recommend to most people without a moment's hesitation. Beyond simple costs, open-source programs also aren't going to change their licensing terms and suddenly lock you out like a paid service could. Open-source software doesn't usually require an account either, though there are a few notable exceptions. Bitwarden The password manager I can always recommend Bitwarden is an open-source password manager with clients for every major desktop operating system and browser. It is capable, easy to use, and free. When you compare it to paid products, you'll find it has most of the same features without worrying about monthly fees and Bitwarden's free tier covers unlimited passwords and devices. Additionally, the code is public and audited, and if you're particularly privacy-conscious, you can self-host a Bitwarden compatible server on your own. The only real trade-off is a simpler UI when compared to programs like 1Password, and a few "quality of life" features like password monitoring (to keep an eye on leaks and breaches) do require an inexpensive subscription. LibreOffice A full office suite for free LibreOffice offers Writer, Calc, and Impress in one convenient package as an alternative to Microsoft's Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Of course, LibreOffice is free and open-source. It has no subscription, requires no accounts, and you don't have to worry about Copilot randomly being inserted during an update you don't want. If you're doing the most common document or spreadsheet tasks, you'll find that LibreOffice is completely up to the job. It even handles DOCX and XLSX files well most of the time. I've only occasionally run into issues with important Excel workbooks, and then only when there were complex automations attached to the spreadsheet. You can download LibreOffice from the official LibreOffice. Make sure to double-check which file format you use—if someone is expecting a DOCX file, you should make sure to send them a DOCX. If you want something that looks a bit more like Microsoft Office, you could try ONLYOFFICE instead. KDE's Kdenlive Great video editing without a subscription or the weird cancellation terms Video editing is a common need these days, but the most powerful tools are locked behind a subscription fee. If you need something basic, Kdenlive is a great option. It offers a timeline-based workflow—much like Adobe Premiere—without any cost. It is a great option for anyone doing light to moderate video editing, including YouTubers, teachers, small business owners, or hobbyists. If you need more advanced color grading tools, I'd recommend checking out DaVInci Resolve rather than jumping straight into a subscription model—DaVinci Resolve is not open-source, but it is free, and its tools are second to none. Make sure to enable hardware encoding the render settings if it isn't already. You'll save yourself a ton of time. GIMP The 3.x update makes GIMP easier to recommend GIMP has had a slightly rocky history. Fortunately, recent releases have significantly improved the program's usability and added new important features, like non-destructive layer effects, that it previously lacked. If you can't justify paying for a Photoshop subscription, but you need to retouch or edit photos, GIMP is a solid option. The big thing you don't get are features like generative fill, which you can replace with local AI models if you really want. GIMP also has a pretty healthy plugin ecosystem, so if it can't do something natively, there is a very good chance you can find a plugin to fill the gap. Audacity Simple, reliable, and it runs on anything Trimming clips, normalizing audio, or removing background noise are all common audio editing tasks, and you don't need a full DAW or Adobe Audition subscription to do it—Audacity will get you 90% of the way there for free. Audacity covers all the basics you'll need for audio editing and is extremely simple to use. The user interface isn't super minimalist either, which means there are fewer functions hidden behind sleek user interfaces. I normally prefer that, since it makes figuring out what an app can actually do a little bit easier. You can't go wrong with recommending a free, open-source tool Recommending paid software always comes with a lot of caveats. If your recommendation falls flat, someone is out of money, and they may be stuck in an agreement with weird cancelation terms. Open-source tools have no such drawbacks. In a worst-case scenario, the open-source tool isn't quite what someone needs, and they move on—no harm done. Most of the time, the free option is perfectly adequate. Always download these apps from their official sites, trusted package managers, or their official GitHub repos. Because these tools are so popular, they are frequently repackaged with adware by third-party sites looking to make a quick buck.

item.title: 5 new PowerToys features that are useful even if you're not a Windows power user
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.48
Microsoft's PowerToys suite of Windows utilities, which you can download from GitHub or install through the Microsoft Store, has earned a reputation as a tool designed for — and used exclusively by — Windows power users. But the reality is more nuanced. Yes, PowerToys includes a number of features you'll probably never need if you're a regular person who uses your Windows PC for entertainment, web browsing, and some light work. But the suite also packs a fair number of utilities that virtually every Windows user will find handy, no matter how "basic" their use of a Windows PC may be. With some of them, I genuinely don't understand why Microsoft hasn't already made them part of vanilla Windows. Since PowerToys recently received a cool new update, I'm going to share five PowerToys features, both old and new, that you should be using even if you don't consider yourself a Windows power user. Power Display Every Windows user with an external display will find this feature handy Ever since I upgraded to an OLED monitor, Power Display has become my favorite PowerToys feature. I recommend it to everyone who uses Windows with an external display, whether it's a desktop PC or a laptop connected to a monitor. through your monitor's menus. Better still, you can also adjust volume, color temperature, input source, and other options by enabling them in the Power Display options menu. These controls work across all the monitors connected to your PC, as well as in both SDR and HDR modes. Personally, I only use the brightness and contrast sliders because that's enough for my needs. Since my monitor is simply too bright for my taste at maximum brightness, I tweak its brightness all the time. When I'm working, I keep it well below 50% (usually at 30% or lower), set it between 60% and 70% when gaming in SDR or watching videos, and crank it up to 100% when playing games in HDR. Without Power Display, I would've had to constantly open the monitor's menu or keep it in HDR mode and constantly reach for the SDR content brightness slider, something I actually did for the first week or so before enabling Power Display. Find My Mouse I'm baffled Microsoft hasn't made this feature available in stock Windows Back when I started using macOS, I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Apple's desktop OS lets you locate your mouse pointer simply by shaking it. It's a very handy feature to have when you're using a 34-inch ultrawide monitor as I do. I eventually found a Windows alternative after installing PowerToys called Find My Mouse, and honestly, I really don't know why Microsoft hasn't added it to vanilla Windows yet. This is something virtually every Windows user could benefit from. If you don't want to mess with extra options, you can simply enable Find My Mouse in the Mouse Utilities menu and choose your preferred activation method. But if you want to go the extra mile, you can adjust the appearance of the mouse spotlight, create a custom activation method, and add excluded apps where the feature won't work while they're in the foreground. Always On Top Pin any window on top of others with a keyboard shortcut Always On Top is another PowerToys module I reckon many regular Windows users will benefit from. It does exactly what it says: it pins a specific app window on top of other windows with a single keyboard shortcut. The pinned window also gets a noticeable border around it, clearly showing that the feature is active. A sound notification also plays when you pin or unpin a window, so you'll always know when a window gets pinned. I usually use it when I need to calculate something with the Calculator app or when I'm writing about an app, such as PowerToys, and want to keep its window visible at all times. I reckon there are countless other scenarios where a feature like this can come in handy, and I'm sure virtually every Windows user will need it sooner or later. So, why don't you download PowerToys and enable it today? Window Hopper Switch between open windows of a single app Window Hopper is a recent addition to PowerToys, and since I’m always juggling multiple browser windows while working, I’ve been using it nonstop ever since Microsoft added it to the suite. It allows you to cycle between windows of a single app, much like the Alt + Tab shortcut lets you switch between all the open windows on your Windows desktop. It's simple and effective, and something I reckon most Windows users will find handy. Peek Preview any file in File Explorer by pressing Space Peek is another simple yet effective PowerToys module that virtually every Windows user can benefit from. Like Quick Look on macOS, which lets you preview files in Finder, Peek allows you to preview files in File Explorer with the press of a button. You can think of it as a minimal photo-viewing app, but Peek is much more powerful. It can open multimedia files, PDFs, HTML, and INI files, show you a summary of folders and files it can't open, and more. It's one of my favorite PowerToys features and yet another PowerToys feature I don't understand why isn't already part of the stock Windows experience. PowerToys is actually really simple to use Don't be daunted by PowerToys and the suite's massive number of modules. Navigating the app is super simple: all you have to do is click a tab, and it will immediately expand to show you all the features inside, which you can then peruse. What I recommend for newcomers is clicking the Welcome to PowerToys button in the lower-left corner, which lists every available feature and explains exactly what it does. After learning about them, you can enable only the ones you want and ignore the ones you don't need. I'm fairly certain you'll discover a few features I didn't mention here that will become indispensable to your daily workflow.

item.title: 4 UniFi mistakes that turn a simple setup into an overcomplicated nightmare
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.14
So, you're wanting to get started with Ubiquiti's UniFi networking gear, huh? I love my UniFi setup, but I definitely made some mistakes. Here are the four biggest mistakes I see people make all the time in the UniFi community, and how you can avoid them. Forgetting to budget for PoE You'll pay for PoE one way or another I love my UniFi setup, but it relies heavily on PoE. At my church, we also run UniFi, and all of the access points there also rely on PoE for power. The problem is, PoE switches are more expensive than non-PoE switches. So, often, a beginner might opt for the cheaper, non-PoE switches to save some cash. However, once you start plugging things in, you'll realize real quick that almost every UniFi accessory needs some form of PoE to run. Access points, doorbells, cameras, and more all require power over ethernet to function. If you don't buy a PoE-capable switch, then you can buy a PoE injector for each area you need power over Ethernet. While this does work, it can quickly add up to be far more expensive than just getting that PoE switch from the start. I personally went used for my PoE switch, and found a 48-port 500W PoE UniFi switch second-hand for $250 shipped and it is more than what I need for my setup, but it gets the job done. Cranking up Wi-Fi power to fix every dead zone More power does not always mean better coverage More power equals better coverage, right? Well, in a sense, yes, but practically, no. You see, with a mesh network like UniFi, more power means that your phone will stay connected to a specific node for longer—often too long. The way mesh networks work is your phone holds onto a node until it reaches a specific connection strength to a node, and then it releases and grabs the next most powerful node that it can. When you crank the power on all your nodes up to high, your phone will stay connected to a node for too long. Just because you have a radio connection to a node doesn't mean you have usable Wi-Fi. So, if your phone reports that it has a high signal strength to a node, it'll stay connected to it, even if you can't actually use the internet. The ideal setup is where your phone releases from a node at right around the furthest distance you can be from it while still using the internet, and then having another node to pick up the slack as soon as you release from the first node. This can take some trial and error. Some nodes might need to be on high power, while others are on low, and others could be somewhere in-between. So, don't default to high power thinking you'll get the best coverage from that—it might actually do the opposite of what you're thinking it will. Copying someone else’s UniFi settings without understanding them Just because it works for someone else's setup doesn't mean it'll work for yours The great part about buying UniFi is there's a robust community surrounding the company's products. However, that isn't always a great thing. Often, people will ask for help with some specific problem, and people will chime in with what fixed it for them. That's great, but those tips shouldn't be taken as the answer. What works for other people should be used as a starting point for finding out what your specific setup needs. This is especially true if you're just getting your information from a YouTube video. Don't get me wrong, I love YouTube tutorials—I make them myself for the maker space. However, tips from a YouTube video should, again, be seen as tips and not instructions on how to fix your exact problem in most instances. So, before you start applying changes from a YouTube video or Facebook group, do some research to understand what those changes are actually changing. Knowing what a setting does will help you better understand how it applies to your own setup, and how to modify it for your needs if it doesn't work first try. Buying for your dream homelab instead of your actual needs Overbuying equipment often leads to an overcomplicated setup I'll admit, I have definitely fallen prey to watching YouTube and building a UniFi cart of all the equipment that I would love to have in my homelab. Then, I quietly empty the cart and walk away, realizing that spending $10,000 on networking equipment isn't the best financial decision. The thing is, finances aren't the only reason it's not best to buy and build your dream homelab before just covering what your needs are. Overbuying equipment often leads to an overcomplicated setup. For instance, your homelab might only need two Wi-Fi nodes and an 8-port switch. However, that 48-port switch looks nice. And the aggregation switch would be good too, right? Don't forget the NVR and NAS, even though you only have one camera and use Dropbox for everything. It all sounds great at first, and sometimes overbuying a little can be helpful, like buying a 16- or 24-port switch instead of 8 so you have room to grow. However, more equipment just adds more maintenance. For instance, at home, I have my Dream Router 7, a 5-port 2.5G switch, my 48-port PoE switch, two Wi-Fi nodes, and one camera. That's it. At my church where I'm about to do a full buildout, I'll have around 8 switches, a Dream Machine Pro Max, an NVR, a NAS, and dozens of both Wi-Fi access points and cameras. Having a big complicated setup makes sense for a 20,000-square-foot church and school, where it doesn't make sense in my 1,300-square-foot home. UniFi is prosumer for a reason The great thing about UniFi is that the equipment is designed for both professional and consumer use cases—hence the term prosumer. There are so many great pieces of UniFi gear to buy, but not everything belongs in a home environment. So, before you spend that big money on that huge cart you've built, step back and think about what your needs actually are. Then, once you've got the equipment you need, make sure to apply the tips I've laid out above for the smoothest experience possible.

item.title: You can now test Nothing’s upcoming devices before launch
item.description:

What you need to know - Nothing’s Community Review Program is back, giving selected fans early access to upcoming products before public launches. - Participants must sign an NDA, respect embargoes, share first impressions, and publish detailed reviews and additional content. - Applications close September 10, but spots aren’t guaranteed, and the program isn’t available to fans in India. Nothing is giving its community another chance to test its upcoming products before anyone else. The company has reopened its Community Review Program, allowing select fans to get hands-on time with Nothing hardware and software before public launches. The program offers select members early access to Nothing products, a direct line to the company, and an opportunity to help shape what it builds next, per the company's announcement. Nothing is particularly interested in applicants with experience in 3D animation, graphic design, music and sound production, and product reviews, but no skills are needed to apply. If you love technology, it's enough. There are some strings attached, though. Because participants may handle unreleased products, they'll need to sign an NDA, follow Nothing's embargo dates, and maintain strict information security. They are also required to give their first impressions of the Nothing Community and social media, publish a full review after launch, and create additional content such as unboxings or product use cases. It’s important to note that being chosen once does not place you on a permanent VIP list. Nothing's previous program terms made clear that participation for one product doesn't guarantee selection for future reviews, so every round is effectively another chance to get in. Review devices are issued under the terms of the current program, so applicants should verify the latest conditions before applying. Nothing will also cover the associated shipping costs. Applications are open until September 10, though selection isn't guaranteed. The program is also unavailable to fans in India. Judging by past instances of this initiative, the brand does indeed implement user feedback. Earlier in 2024, Nothing had a public campaign called “The Community Edition Project” for the Nothing Phone 2a. Over several months, the company asked its community to submit designs for the phone's hardware, wallpapers, packaging, and marketing. item.title: These popular Samsung phones just received their final software update
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.51
What you need to know - Samsung has officially ended software support for the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 after five years. - Both foldables received four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates, as Samsung originally promised. - Samsung has removed both phones from its security update page, meaning they won't receive regular security patches anymore. Samsung's foldable phones that launched in the summer of 2021 have officially reached the end of their software support cycle. Most Samsung flagship smartphones today, including the Galaxy S26 Ultra and even 2024's Galaxy S24 Ultra, come with seven years of software support. But Samsung hasn't always offered updates for this long. Older flagships came with shorter support promises, and now the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have officially reached the end of theirs. As spotted by Android Authority, the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have received their final software updates. At launch, Samsung promised four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates for both foldables, and the company has now fulfilled that promise. Samsung has also removed both devices from its security updates page. This means Samsung won't be releasing any further regular software or security updates for these devices. The oldest foldables officially supported by the company are now the Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Galaxy Z Flip 4. Even those devices have moved to a quarterly update schedule, unlike newer Samsung phones that continue to receive monthly updates. So, if you're still using a Galaxy Z Fold 3 or Galaxy Z Flip 3, your phone won't receive any new regular security patches from Samsung going forward. That means any new security vulnerabilities discovered from here on may remain unpatched on these devices. If you're still holding onto one of these foldables, this might finally be the time to start thinking about an upgrade. Samsung recently introduced a completely new form factor with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, while its latest foldables also come with a much longer software support promise. If you've managed to keep your Fold 3 or Flip 3 running for five years, one of Samsung's newer foldables should last you considerably longer. item.title: I found something better than the Bose QC Ultra Gen II: meet Noble's FoKus Amadeus
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.27
There's extensive choice if you want to get a pair of decent earbuds. Bose, Sennheiser, and Sony continue to be heavy-hitters in this category (I use my Bose QuietComfort Ultra Gen II while traveling), and phone brands also a good job with their earbuds — Google's Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro deliver a vibrant sound with plenty of useful features. But if you want the best sound quality, you'll need to turn your attention to Noble Audio. The boutique brand is known for its IEMs, and it has ventured into wireless earbuds in recent years. I've heard plenty of great things about the brand, so I was excited to get my hands on the FoKus Amadeus. Retailing for $320 on Amazon, the Amadeus is in the similar price bracket as the Bose QC Ultra Gen II and Sony WF-1000XM6, but what you're getting here is markedly different. For starters, the design of the FoKus Amadeus is unlike any other earbuds around. Mainstream brands play it pretty safe with their designs, and they're not meant to stand out — that isn't the case here. With a bright red design and a custom shell that's bigger than most earbuds, these are guaranteed to grab attention. Like the Amadeus name, the red design is an homage to Mozart’s signature tailcoat, says Noble. Build quality is great, and while the size of the shell means the earbuds jut out, I didn't see any issues with comfort. Each bud weighs 7g, and that's in line with other products in this category. The only omission is ingress protection, so I wouldn't suggest using these at the gym. Just like the buds, the case itself is bigger, but the square design makes it easy to take anywhere. Coming to connectivity, the Amadeus gets Bluetooth 5.4 via Qualcomm’s QCC3091 modem, and there's SBC, AAC, LDAC, and AptX Adaptive. The buds connect to two devices at once, and I had no problems pairing with my Pixel 11 Pro XL, Find X9 Ultra, and iPad Pro M4. There's good ANC as well, and the buds did a great job tuning out the ambient sounds in my surroundings. Obviously, sound quality is where the Amadeus excels. The sound signature from the 8.3mm dynamic driver is tuned towards musicality, and you get a good bass rumble with clean mids and a nice treble extension. These are particularly great with vocals, and the soundstage is significantly wider than any other earbuds in this category. There's a level of dynamism to the sound that you just don't get with Bose or Sony, and that ultimately makes the Amadeus enjoyable even in extended listening sessions. Another thing I like is the sheer level of customizability to the sound. Noble uses Audiodo to tune the sound of the Amadeus to your individual preferences. This is done by a listening test that lasts up to three minutes, and then you get a custom EQ that's tailored to your ears. The tech works exceedingly well, and it makes a big difference to the sound. In addition to Audiodo, you get a 10-band EQ and custom modes that let you tweak the sound profile to a granular degree. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Then there's the app; the Noble FoKus app has to be the best of any buds I used. You get a minimal interface without any overt styling (looking at you, Sennheiser), but there's an extensive amount of customizability when it comes to adjusting the sound. I got good battery life as well. The Amadeus lasted close to eight hours between charges, and each bud has a 65mAh battery. The case provides an additional 2.5 times charge via a 500mAh battery, so you get just around 40 hours before you'll need to plug in the case. There is fast charging that gives you two hours of music with a 10-minute charge, and a full charge takes just over 90 minutes. I know that's $320 is at the higher end of the scale when it comes to earbuds, and to its credit, Noble Audio didn't omit anything in the FoKus Amadeus. The design stands out quite a bit, but the earbuds are comfortable to wear, and the sound quality is outstanding; if you've used Bose's QC Ultra or any of Sony's earbuds, you will see an immediate difference when switching to these — I did. The FoKus Amadeus is designed to stand out, and the sound quality is immersive like no other earbuds in this category. When Dbrand told me it was launching a new minimalist case sub-brand, I was immediately interested. The burgundy is my favorite of the four, although I think it looks terrible on an orange iPhone. Better stick to black or tan for a bolder color like that. Dbrand sent me cases for the Pixel 11 Pro and the iPhone Pro Max 17/18 (since they're the same phone anyway). The "sandstone" texture on these isn't at all like OnePlus's sandstone phones or cases — meaning they're textured but not rough like sandstone usually is — which gives it a nice grip without sanding your fingerprints off by accident. I also love the clicky covered buttons on the case. It's got all the port cutouts you'd hope to find on a case, plus a perfectly sized lip around the front glass to protect it. I didn't have trouble using gestures with these cases, unlike some rugged cases that have too large a lip and usually get in the way. These also aren't minimalist in the way Thinborne cases are. They're not super rugged like Dbrand's Tank cases are, but they still add a little bit of bulk to the phone. They're cushy and a few millimeters thin, but they weigh around 40-50g, depending on the phone, which is roughly twice the weight of an aramid fiber case (like Thinborne). The bright side to the extra "bulk" is that these are more drop-resistant than aramid fiber cases. I purposefully dropped the Pixel 11 Pro on the concrete from about 3ft up a few times to see what would happen. The phone looked untouched, and the MNML case just had a few minor dings on the corners. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Seems to me that these will generally hold up nicely to wear and tear over the life of your phone, making them a great option to grab the next time you're in a Best Buy (so long as you don't care about Dbrand skins). Dbrand makes MNML cases for 24 phone models across Apple, Samsung, and Google Pixel phone lines. That MNML sub-brand also includes a handful of MagSafe accessories, like a kickstand wallet, slim wallet, and an AirPods case (I guess that's a thing?). item.title: Ukraine's army is turning Humvees into remote-controlled vehicles connected by Starlink
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 4.97
- Ukrainian firm Drone Fight Group has delivered three Humvees fitted with its Kaban remote-control kit - The Kaban kit bolts on without modifying the vehicle's structure, allowing crews to switch between remote and manual modes depending on their needs - The primary control link here is Starlink, with analog video and radio communication as a fallback, in addition to an automatic stop if connections are not found Ukraine has begun converting American-supplied Humvees into remotely operated ground vehicles using a bolt-on kit that leaves the original vehicle intact and routes its control signals through Starlink. The system is called Kaban, Ukrainian for "boar." Developer Drone Fight Group says it has delivered three converted High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicles to Ukrainian formations: the 3rd Army Corps, the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment "Achilles," and the 49th Brigade. With over 5,000 Humvees in service in Ukraine thanks to US military aid and grants, the Kaban retrofit could have far-reaching impacts in a war zone where automation is increasingly being used on both sides. What does Kaban offer the Ukrainian military? Rather than designing a purpose-built robot and waiting for it to reach production, Kaban turns existing hardware units into an unmanned platform on demand. This is crucial in a war where economics dictate much of the conflict, and both sides often have to repurpose aging military hardware to meet their needs. Kaban installs without modifying the vehicle's structure, and operators can switch between remote and manual driving. This is crucial, as a converted Humvee is still essentially a manually driven vehicle with an add-on, and a crew can physically drive it when the mission requires a person behind the wheel. SpaceX's Starlink functions as the primary control link for Kaban deployments. The system also supports analog video transmission and radio control as backup channels, letting it hedge its bets in an environment where any single link can be blocked or targeted, rendering devices that rely on it useless. From the control station, an operator gets vehicle movement plus headlights, infrared illumination, searchlights, two-way audio, and telemetry from the vehicle's onboard computer. Navigation runs on a digital map where the operator plots routes and drops markers, with a predicted trajectory overlay to help maneuver the Humvee. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! If the on-device GPS is jammed or spoofed, which is a routine occurrence near the line of contact, the operator can correct the vehicle's position manually instead of losing it to attackers. If the link fails entirely, however, Kaban brings the vehicle to an automatic stop. The move to a satellite link is a paradigm shift on a battlefield that has recently relied heavily on short-range radio or spooled fiber, both of which require the controller to be nearby. The satellite link essentially lets operators deploy and control military hardware from a much greater distance, improving their safety. Optional equipment the Kaban can come with for retrofitted Humvees includes thermal cameras, searchlights, net launchers to catch incoming drones, and platforms for launching Ukraine's own drones, making it a highly versatile option on the battlefield. The news comes as the world sees a massive ramp-up in Ukrainian ground robotics. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense recorded more than 100,000 UGV logistics and evacuation missions in 2026 till August 20, logged in the DELTA combat management system. Most of those, however, are purpose-built platforms that concentrate on one particular aspect of the military's needs. Kaban bets that the faster route to fleet-scale automation runs through the vehicles a military already owns, a proposition that could have an impact far beyond the Russia-Ukraine war, as militaries worldwide continue to observe the conflict.
