item.title: RIP Ubisoft Connect? New Tool Replaces Game Launcher, Only on 1 Game to Start
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.80
Starting with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, gamers will no longer need the Ubisoft Connect PC game launcher, but can instead tap a new Ubisoft Connect Services Steam tool. The tool "keeps Ubisoft game features such as cross-progression, cross-play, player safety, challenges and rewards, among others, without requiring the Ubisoft Connect PC launcher to be installed or launched," the company says. "This first version is an initial step toward a smoother and more streamlined launch experience on Steam," Ubisoft adds. "We will continue to iterate and improve Ubisoft Connect Services over time, with the goal of delivering the features and services players use and expect while making the Steam experience as seamless as possible." Monopolies aren't ideal, and Steam shouldn't control everything, but I don't know anyone who enjoys having to use Ubisoft Connect to launch Assassin's Creed games, or EA's app to play Need for Speed. I love GoG, and think the GoG Galaxy client is quite nice, but even I can't be bothered to open it up to play a different collection of games. So, I'm quite excited that Ubisoft is finally making it so you don't have to log in to Ubisoft Connect after logging into Steam to play Prince of Persia. Of course, this is probably a way to make Ubisoft's games more playable on alternative platforms like the Steam Machine, which use translation layers like Proton. Ditching the secondary login systems of Ubisoft Connect and similar third-party stores and account systems ensures Ubisoft titles are more accessible and likely saves Ubisoft customer support a lot of accessibility headaches in the future. The comments on the Steam thread are almost universally positive. Some even say it will encourage them to start buying Ubisoft games again, so the goodwill (which Ubisoft could always use) may translate into a financial benefit for Ubisoft, too. However, others urged caution. They highlight that family sharing may still fail to work effectively with Ubisoft games, because the underlying Connect service should be the same. It will likely still mean a demand for online connection to play even "offline," single-player games. I'm not as concerned by that as I once was. When I occasionally have internet outages, it can be extremely aggravating, but that only happens once or twice a year. Removing a secondary login step at least is a step in the right direction. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Anthropic Blocked 5 Possible Attempts to Research Bioweapons With Claude AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.79
Anthropic’s latest threat intelligence report details seven ways the AI company has found its models being misused, including five instances of research related to biological weapons development in unnamed countries. The 154-page report dives deep into dangerous activities in use between December 2025 and August 2026. Topics also include conventional weapons development, cyber operations, distillation, influence campaigns, scams and fraud, and surveillance. The scenarios used various Claude models, including versions of Haiku, Opus, and Sonnet. The only use of Anthropic's most advanced Fable and Mythos models was a single case of distillation, the practice of using top AI models to train less advanced rivals. Each scenario detailed in the report was addressed by Anthropic, including banning the user, implementing further safeguards, and reporting relevant criminal activity to the authorities. The report included five case studies where Anthropic believes actors may have used its models to “support biological weapons development.” The scenarios include someone planning avian influenza mammalian-adaptation experiments and another party working with Claude to redesign toxins while attempting to keep their identity vague. Anthropic said, "Actors circumvented controls we impose to prevent users from unsupported regions accessing our models, and engaged in other efforts to obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The brand said it kept the countries of origin and the research institutions' identities hidden in this report, as it cannot confirm whether the scientists' experiments were conducted with the intent to cause harm. It notes how biological research can be dual-use: running these experiments may not necessarily be malicious and may be part of research toward a vaccine or a cure for a disease. Other elements of Anthropic's report indicate that bad actors regularly use Claude to help with cyberattacks and security breaches. Those instances included state-sponsored groups, politically motivated individuals, and other financially motivated criminals. It also found six scenarios where Claude was being used to develop software for weapons, including “firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them". Anthropic said, “We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses." This report comes a few days after a public resignation from Anthropic, in which AI researcher Jacob Coxon said the company and its rival, OpenAI, are not "acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Anthropic's Evan Hubinger, who works on AI safety, reposted the message saying, "We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think this is >10% within the next decade." Hubinger continued, "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." When asked about the threat posed by AI, US President Donald Trump said on Thursday, "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period." On X, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) said, "Washington needs to wake up and take this seriously." Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also told The View, "We cannot stick our heads in the sand and pretend this technology isn’t happening. We need guardrails. But America needs to lead.” About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: 'We Need to Slow Down': AI Crowd Reacts to Viral Human Extinction Warning
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.65
Artificial intelligence researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and posted a rallying cry on X this week about the dangers of AI. Less than 72 hours later, the post had been seen by over 164 million people, prompting reactions from the AI rank-and-file and CEOs. Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, says both companies aren’t acting responsibly. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he wrote. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Notably, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, quote-tweeted Coxon's post in support of the message soon after it was posted. “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," Hubinger wrote. He also cited a recent report showing that while Anthropic believes the risk of catastrophe is low, self-improving models could drastically change the situation. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI has commented publicly on Coxon’s statements. But the post has over 780,000 likes, moving beyond the AI-focused tech sphere to a much wider audience. Other Anthropic employees have felt free to comment. Ethan Perez, who works on the alignment team and helped to hire Coxon, said he is a “strong researcher," adding, “Before he left, I pitched him to stay and join my team, and I was sad he decided to leave, as are many of my colleagues. 100% agree with him that AI poses serious risks to society, and I'm glad he's speaking out!" Julie Steele, who works on the safety research team at OpenAI, posted a simple message of support. “I work at OpenAI. In my personal capacity, I also think we need to slow down.” Jasmine Wang, who works on alignment and safety at OpenAI, also agreed with Coxon's comments, writing, "A solid proportion of folks across labs have signed a petition saying we need to pace, many of them directly working on safety." 'Seems Like a Setup' Not every AI expert believes Coxon's message is an accurate picture. OpenAI employee Chris Hayduk said, “I work at OpenAI and personally think AI has been and will continue to be an extremely beneficial technology to humanity.” He believes the conversation should instead be framed around how it will “save” billions of lives. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue said Coxon’s opinion on safety isn’t helpful, although he separately advocates increasing research into the existential risks posed by AI. “Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se, but let’s keep things in perspective and hear from the full range of expertise across the ecosystem!” Hugging Face's AI platform was recently hacked by OpenAI agents that broke into its systems to access a database. The company was later acquired by Nvidia for $12.9 billion. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly told attendees at a Goldman Sachs event on Thursday that Coxon's claims are "deeply untrue," adding that Coxon is ignorant of all the work being done around the industry to drive safety, according to Altimeter founder Brad Gerstner, who attended Huang's talk at the conference. Elon Musk also took to his social network to say he believes Coxon's narrative "seems like a setup.” In follow-up messages, he noted that Coxon only worked at Anthropic for a few months before leaving. Fuel for the Coming Political Fight No matter your take on Coxon's warning, it has become a lightning rod for the conversation around the future of AI regulation in the US. Multiple political figures have debated AI regulation plans over the last 48 hours, citing Coxon's viral message. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) posted to X, "Washington needs to wake up and take this seriously." Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-Vt.) said, "The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity. That is why I will soon be introducing legislation to ban superintelligence and pause AI development." Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told The View, "We cannot stick our heads in the sand and pretend this technology isn’t happening. We need guardrails. But America needs to lead.” Someone who isn't concerned about the safety of AI is US President Donald Trump, who said on Thursday, "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period." Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: 19 Years Ago, We Predicted the iPhone Would Lead to 'Some Insanely Great Products.' It Sure Did
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.42
Editors' Note: Welcome to our ongoing An Apple a Day series, where we’ll share Apple stories and video from our archives daily from now through late September. In addition to PCMag, this series includes pieces from our sibling sites CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, and Popular Science. The excitement surrounding the original iPhone was electric. From the moment Apple CEO Steve Jobs held the product on stage at Macworld in January 2007 until it reached Apple and AT&T retail stores in June, the iPhone captivated the entire tech sphere. The six-month timespan in between felt like an eternity. Even before it was released, the iPhone was loved and reviled equally. Some hailed it as the "Jesus phone," a device to save us all from tech drudgery, while others judged it more for what it wasn't than what it was. Whether you were an early believer or not, the first iPhone's release was a watershed moment that emphatically shoved the industry in a new direction. Looking back at the review (which you can read in full here), it's amazing to see how on-point it was, despite some skepticism from our expert reviewers. "The Apple iPhone is a great first try from Apple," Sascha Segan and Tim Gideon noted. They added, "Apple's smart, though, and this is just the beginning. Think of this as the 128K Mac of the 21st century—a vanguard product, maybe not perfect or the most usable machine ever...but heralding some insanely great products to come." How the Industry Largely Wrote the iPhone Off I still vividly remember the iPhone pre-release news cycles. At the time, I was a writer for a small website called Phonescoop. Apple announced the iPhone in San Francisco on January 9, when most of the industry was in Las Vegas for CES. The next day, I actually sat with PCMag's then-lead phone reviewer, Sascha Segan, at the Hilton in Las Vegas, at a joint press briefing held by Apple and its network partner, AT&T. The small group peppered the Apple and AT&T folks with questions during a sometimes contentious session. Sascha loudly questioned Apple's decision to ship the phone with EDGE (2.5G) rather than UMTS or CDMA (3G), which was catching on with many competing devices at the time. On paper, the original iPhone was sort of a loser in the eyes of the tech-obsessed. It lacked so much technology compared with the BlackBerrys, Communicators, Treos, and Windows Mobile devices of the day. It didn't have 3G, didn't support stereo Bluetooth, couldn't run third-party apps, and the stated one-day battery life was less than half the endurance of others. It packed a 2MP camera with a single function at a time when Nokia was shipping advanced 5MP cameras with multiple capture modes. The original iPhone couldn't send picture messages, nor could it record video at launch. The industry largely wrote it off. "There's no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share," said Microsoft's then-CEO, Steve Ballmer. It took 74 days for Apple to sell 1 million of them. And things only exploded from there. This week, Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, the 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable phone, the Duo. Not a Very Good Phone, But It Did Change Everything In person, it turns out, the device was remarkable in many ways. It was the first phone to have only a finger-touch user interface. Until then, most devices relied on resistive screens that supported stylus input but still required directional buttons or scroll wheels to navigate. And while the iPhone wasn't the first phone to support multi-point touch (up to 10 fingers at a time), it was the first to put it to such effective use, with swiping and pinching gestures that moved you through the home screen and menus. We all still use this UI paradigm every single day. Meanwhile, the iPod app's UI was colorful, fun, and just so different from text-heavy, folder-based menus on every other device. And, despite its limitations, browsing the web on Safari was worlds different from the text-heavy WAP browsers on many other phones, thanks to its broader support for HTML and imagery. Segan captured all this in his initial review, co-written with then audio reviewer Tim Gideon. "The seamless integration of the internet, iPod, Maps, Phone, and email functions flaunted in the commercials is no exaggeration," they wrote. "The iPhone is intuitive, interconnected, and impossible to get lost in—just hit the home button to get to the main screen." Enamored as he was with the user interface, Segan didn't hold back about the iPhone's faults: "It isn't a very good phone. Call quality was the worst we've heard on a high-end device in years." "What sort of smartphone doesn't have corporate email?" critics quipped.
The iPhone was widely panned for its limited support for enterprise email and messaging, features considered vital to the smartphone-toting crowd of the era (mostly traveling professionals). PIM (personal information management) was the crux of Research In Motion's and Microsoft's mobile businesses at the time, and licensing access to Exchange was big money. "What sort of smartphone doesn't have corporate email?" critics quipped. There's no doubt the first iPhone had many limitations, but plenty of people saw it for the new dynamic it introduced. And it did change everything. For the next year, LG, Motorola, and Samsung tripped over themselves to create "iPhone killers," and they all failed for one reason or another. Nokia, RIM, and Microsoft could hardly be bothered to respond. It wasn't until Google launched Android in October 2008 that a truly competitive platform arrived. PCMag's initial review was well-informed, praised the phone on its merits, and docked points where it came up short. The original iPhone was not the most technically advanced device of its day, but it offered one of the best experiences, merged multiple products into one (phone, music player, camera), and shook things up in just the right way. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Managing Editor for Consumer Electronics content, overseeing an experienced team of reviewers and product testers. I’ve been covering technology for more than 25 years. Prior to PCMag, I worked at outlets such as Android Authority, Fortune, InformationWeek, and Phonescoop.

item.title: Is It Worth It to Upgrade to Switch 2 Games? We'll Run You Through the Actual Costs
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.42
Video game prices have been slowly creeping up for years. When the Nintendo Switch first launched in 2017, full-priced games were $60. Then, PlayStation and Xbox first-party releases jumped to $70 in 2020. Nintendo followed suit in 2023 with The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. But Switch 2 pricing has made everything more complicated. Mario Kart World costs $80. Donkey Kong Bananza is $70. Yet Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is just $40. Want to buy physical games? That will cost you more than the digital versions. And even though some of the Switch 1 games I own are backward compatible, if I want to upgrade to the Switch 2 version for better performance or additional DLC, the upgrade pricing is all over the place. In some cases, upgrading costs $0, while others require you to break out your credit card. Here's the full breakdown of how much it costs to upgrade your old Switch game to the Switch 2 versions. The 3 Types of Switch 2 Games Before I talk about how much the upgrades cost, I need to explain the three (yes, three) different kinds of games you can play on the Switch 2. - Switch 2 games: These are native Switch 2 games made exclusively for the console. They feature the Switch 2 logo and are designed to take advantage of the latest hardware. This includes Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza, as well as third-party releases like Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition. - Switch 2 Edition games: These are Switch games that have performance and visual upgrades over their Switch 1 counterparts. The physical versions of these titles will have the Switch game and Upgrade Pack on the same cartridge. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A are Switch 2 Edition games, and are labeled accordingly. - Switch 1 games: Finally, there are just Switch 1 games, since (most of) these can be played on the Switch 2. This means you can play Breath of the Wild or Metroid Dread for free if you already own those games. They won't have the significant upgrades that come with the Upgrade Packs, but should gain some small benefits simply by running on more powerful hardware. How Much Does Nintendo Charge for a Switch 2 Upgrade Pack? Instead of having to buy new games to get upgraded versions of the titles you already own, Nintendo allows you to upgrade your Switch games into native Switch 2 games, turning them into Switch 2 Edition games. However, the cost of that upgrade varies widely, depending on how much new content is included. - $20: Upgrade Packs that include DLC-sized additions for the Switch 2 cost $20. This includes Super Mario Party Jamboree, Kirby and the Forgotten Land, and Super Mario Bros. Wonder, which add new gameplay features and content to the base game. The Switch 2 Edition versions of these games cost $80, so it's the $60 base game + $20 DLC. - $10: Games with smaller performance and visual upgrades, such as Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A, cost $10. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are also priced here because a new copy of BOTW for Switch 2 costs $70 and TOTK costs $80. However, they're actually included as part of Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack. It's interesting to note that the Xenoblade games add some additional content. - The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild - The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Metroid Prime 4: Beyond - Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy - Pokémon Legends: Z-A - Xenoblade Chronicles: Definitive Edition - Xenoblade Chronicles 2 - Xenoblade Chronicles 3 - $5: Nintendo introduced a $5 upgrade path for the Switch 2 Edition of Animal Crossing: New Horizons to coincide with the game's free version 3.0 update. This upgrade adds enhanced visuals, GameChat functionality, and mouse controls. Xenoblade Chronicles X is another $5 upgrade, but it just includes performance improvements. Interestingly, both games are getting new physical editions, so is this the one common thread? - Free: Finally, some games have received free updates from Nintendo, including Arms, Pokémon Scarlet/Violet, The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom, Super Mario Odyssey, Bowser's Fury, and more. These updates mainly focus on visual upgrades, though some gain frame rate bumps, HDR, and even GameChat support. - Arms - Animal Crossing: New Horizons - Big Brain Academy: Brain vs. Brain - Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker - Clubhouse Games: 51 Worldwide Classics - Donkey Kong Country Returns HD - Game Builder Garage - The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom - The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening - Mario Kart 8 Deluxe - New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe - Pikmin 3 Deluxe - Pokémon Champions - Pokémon Scarlet and Violet - Splatoon 3 - Super Mario: 3D World + Bowser's Fury - Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2 - Super Mario Odyssey How Much Are Third-Party Games? It's not just Nintendo games that have unlockable updates for the Switch 2; all developers have the option of offering an upgrade path to players. Many of these updates come with graphic and performance improvements, but some may add additional content. However, how much this costs will depend on the game and the publisher. For instance, games in Hamster's Arcade Archives line cost $2.99 to upgrade. Meanwhile, Marvelous has multiple games at the $10 price point. However, many developers have opted not to charge for the Switch 2 Edition of their game. This means if you own the Switch version of the game, the upgrade pack is available to you as a free download. - 1000xResist - Free - 4PGP - $5 - A-Train: All Aboard! Tourism - $7 - Another Crab's Treasure - Free - Another Eden Begins - $5 - Asdivine Knot - $1 - Asphalt Legends - Free - Atelier Yumia: The Alchemist of Memories & the Envisioned Land - $10 - Ball x Pit - Free - Bang! Bang! Bandits - $3 - Beyblade X Evobattle - $10 - BlazBlue Entropy Effect X - $2 - Blood Dungeon - Free - Blood: Refreshed Supply - Free - Botany Manor - $4 - Braid: Anniversary Edition - $3 - Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged - $5 - Brotato - Free - Card-en-Ciel - $10 - Cast n Chill - Free - Chippy&Noppo - $2.40 - Citizen Sleeper - Free - Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector - Free - Core Keeper - Free - Cozy Grove - Free - Cozy Grove: Camp Spirit - Free - Culdcept Begins - $10 - Dark Auction - $1 - Dave the Diver - Free - Deltarune - Free - Demon Castle Story - $4 - Dinkum - Free - Disney Dreamlight Valley - Free - Disney Speedstorm - Free - Dispatch - Free - Divinity: Original Sin II - Free - Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake - Free - Dream Town Island - $4 - The Drifter - Free - Dungeon Village 2 - $4 - Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Anniversary Edition - Free - The Exit 8 - $1 - Factorio - Free - Fantasy Life i: The Girl Who Steals Time - $2.59 - Final Fantasy Tactics - The Ivalice Chronicles - Free - Fitness Boxing 3: Your Personal Trainer - $10 - The Fox's Way Home - $3 - Fruit Mountain Party - $1.88 - Game Dev Story - $4 - Go-Go Town - $3 - Gunvolt Chronicles: Luminous Avenger iX 1+2 Dual Collection - $5 - Hades II - Free - Hello Kitty Island Adventure - $10 - High on Life - Free - Hogwarts Legacy - $10 - Hollow Knight - Free - Hollow Knight: Silksong - Free - Human Fall Flat - $5 - Inazuma Eleven: Victory Road - $2.59 - Isekai Rondo - $1 - Isekai Villain - $1 - It Takes Two - Free - Jumbo Airport Story - $4 - Kingdom's Return: Time-Eating Fruit and the Ancient Monster - Kuukiyomi 4: Consider It - $5 - Lego Party! - Free - Little Rocket Lab - Free - Lollipop Chainsaw RePop - $5 - Lorelei and the Laser Eyes - Free - Lou's Lagoon - Free - Lynked: Banner of the Spark - Free - Memory of Memorie : A Chill Story - $2 - Mina the Hollower - Free - Minecraft - Coming soon - Minishoot' Adventures - Free - Moonlight Peaks - $5 - Nicktoons & The Dice of Destiny - Free - No Man's Sky - Free - Novel Rogue - $1 - Once Upon a Katamari - Free - One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 - Free - Overcooked 2! - $10 - Outlaws + Handful of Missions: Remaster - Free - Overrogue - $1 - Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo - Free - Planet of Lana II - Free - The Prince of Tennis Doki Doki Survival - $5 - The Prince of Tennis Sweet School Festival - $5 - Pritto Prisoner - $1 - Psyvariar 3 - Free - R-Type Tactics I • II Cosmos - $5 - The Ramen Sensei - $4 - Red Dead Redemption - Free - RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic - $5 - Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven - $10 - The Rumble Fish 2 - $5 - Rune Factory: Guardians of Azuma - $10 - Sail Forth - Free - Sayonara Wild Hearts - Free - Shadow Labyrinth - Free - Shuten Order - $2.49 - Sid Meier's Civilization VII - $10 - Simogo Legacy Collection - Skyship Quest Story - $4 - Soma - Free - Sonic Racing: Crossworlds - $10 - Stardew Valley - Free - Storm Lancers - Free - Story of Seasons: Grand Bazaar - $10 - Subnautica - Free - Subnautica: Below Zero - Free - Super Bomberman Collection - $5 - System Shock Remake - Free - System Shock 2: 25th Anniversary Remaster - Free - Tales of the Shire: A The Lord of the Rings Game - Free - Tamagotchi Plaza - $10 - Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate - $2.49 - Tomb Raider I-III Remastered - Free - Touhou Yukkuri Mountain - $1.50 - Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter - $1 - Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter - $5 - The Touryst - $6 - Unrailed 2: Back on Track - Free - Wobbly Life - $5 - Woodo - Free Not All Games Have Upgrade Paths Keep in mind that not all titles will offer upgrade paths. Square Enix, for instance, seems to shy away from making the Switch and Switch 2 versions of their games compatible or upgradeable. Some Sega games do the same. That has also typically meant save data can't be carried over either, so be careful before buying a game on Switch that you plan to upgrade down the road on Switch 2. You'll need to re-buy these games—at full price—to get them on the new console: - Atelier Ryza Secret Trilogy Deluxe Pack - Dragon Quest I & II HD-2D Remake - Dragon Quest VII: Reimagined - Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age - Definitive Edition - Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim - Owners can buy Anniversary Edition for $20 - Final Fantasy Resonance - Final Fantasy X & X-2 HD Remaster - Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity - Owners can buy Definitive Edition at a discount - No Sleep For Kaname Date - From AI: The Somnium Files - Nobunaga's Ambition: Awakening - Octopath Traveler - Octopath Traveler 2 - Octopath Traveler 0 - Raidou Remastered - Shinobi: Art of Vengeance - Sonic Frontiers - Definitive Edition - Sonic X Shadow Generations - Star Ocean: The Second Story R - Suika Game Planet - Suikoden I & II HD Remaster Other games may also receive free patches that allow them to take advantage of the new hardware without the need for a true upgrade path. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Series 11: What's the Difference?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.17
Table of Contents The first foldable iPhone might be the biggest announcement to come out of Apple's September event, but there were plenty of other reveals, including new Apple Watches. Replacing the Editors' Choice-winning Apple Watch Series 11 from last year is the new Series 12. Apple is going even harder on AI and health tracking with this new smartwatch, debuting a range of new features enabled Apple's S11 chip. Let's compare to see if it's worth upgrading from the Series 11 to the Series 12. Full Specs | Apple Watch Series 12 | Apple Watch Series 11 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S10 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 24 hours (estimated) | 43 hours (tested) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: A Slight Increase on the Larger 46mm Model Not many changes to price year over year, but the newer watch is slightly more expensive if you have a big wrist. The Series 12 starts at $399 for a 42mm aluminum body sans cellular service, just like the Series 11. It scales up more quickly, though, with the larger 46mm version adding $50 versus the 46mm Series 11's $30 premium. Either way, adding cellular service is the same $100 for both generations. You can also upgrade to a titanium version with cellular in 42mm for $699 and 46mm for $749, also the same as the Series 11. The Series 12 adds a new ceramic design that's even pricier at $899 and $949 for the small and large sizes, respectively, but that's better explored in the next section. Regardless, you can expect to see discounts on the Series 11 for as long as retailers have stock (the 46mm aluminum GPS-only model is currently available on Amazon for $329). If you can wait until a sales event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, Apple Watches also typically see pretty big, usually temporary, price cuts around those times. Winner: Apple Watch Series 11 Design: Fresh New Finishes for the Series 12 The two Apple Watches look nearly identical in shape, though the aluminum and titanium Series 12 are just a millimeter wider and 1.5 grams heavier than their Series 11 counterparts. The color choices for them are slightly different, with the aluminum Series 12 swapping out silver and rose gold finishes for light gold and bronze, and titanium adding a radiant gold version. Then there's the ceramic version, in white or blue. It adds another millimeter to the watch's height, width, and depth, and another six to eight grams in weight. Apparently, dark blue ceramic is just very slightly heavier than white ceramic. Either way, you have more options with the Series 12. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 AI Features: Say What, Siri? The Series 12 uses Apple's new S11 chip to enable Apple Intelligence features that the Series 11 lacks. The biggest addition is Audio Intelligence, a feature that lets the Series 12 listen to everything around you all day, providing summaries of conversations and even rewinding parts to help you catch up. It can also recognize important sounds like alarms and doorbells to notify you of them if you're hard of hearing. Myself, I'm leery of this type of always-listening feature on any device, but Apple claims the S11 chip protects privacy with hardware-isolated onboard audio processing. It also says Audio Intelligence doesn't identify speakers and doesn't include identifying information in its output. If you're still uncertain, though, you can just turn the feature off. The Series 11 doesn't support Audio Intelligence at all (but there's still all the standard hands-free Siri functionality and other, less intrusive Apple Intelligence features). Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Health and Fitness: Improved Sensors Deliver 24x More Data The Series 12 makes some big leaps in fitness and health tracking features. Apple has reworked its optical and electrical heart rate sensors, and now the watch measures your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day instead of only periodically, as the Series 11 does. The new watch also measures heart rate variability up to 24 times more often, with a new section of the Heart Rate app dedicated to the data. Apple claims it's the most accurate heart rate tracking in a wearable. Apple is also taking a more holistic approach to fitness with a new Apple Intelligence-powered readiness score that provides a number from 0 to 10 assessing your energy for the day, with a recommendation to go all-out, pace yourself, or rest and recover. These kinds of scores and recommendations are already available on Google and Samsung's smartwatches and other wearables, and they can be helpful if you just want a general sense of your current health state and how hard you should work out. The readiness score is exclusive to the Series 12, though the Series 11 offers other holistic scores for sleep and mindfulness. Outside of the improved heart rate sensors and readiness score, the Series 12 and Series 11 are equally equipped for general health and fitness. Both support on-demand blood oxygen and ECG readings, keep tabs on your sleep, and offer all the other fitness-tracking tools that are now standard in most smartwatches. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Battery Life: Same Estimate, Potential Real-World Differences Apple claims the Series 12 can last up to 24 hours between charges with normal use, but the company is usually very conservative with battery life estimates. The Series 11 has the same claimed 24-hour battery life, but in our real-world testing, it lasted 43 hours with the always-on display enabled. However, the new heart rate tracker's continuous activity could shorten real-world battery life, bringing it closer to Apple's estimate. We won't know until we actually test the Series 12. Winner: To Be Determined Durability: A New Ceramic Display Coating The Series 12 has the same IP6X dustproof rating and is water-resistant to up to 164 feet, just like the Series 11. The aluminum version is a bit tougher, though, thanks to its new Ceramic Shield 2 glass (different from the ceramic case option), which Apple claims is 60% more durable than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11. The titanium models can probably take equal beatings, and it's safe to say the ceramic version of the watch is also pretty sturdy. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Connectivity: Dual-Band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and Optional 5G No changes here between Apple Watch generations. Both the Series 11 and Series 12 have dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, and L1 GPS standard, along with Apple's Ultra Wideband chip for precisely tracking the watch's nearby location with your phone. The cellular versions also have the same 5G and LTE radios. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Series 12 The Apple Watch Series 12 delivers some fitness and AI improvements that could make it a significant upgrade over the Series 11, which, while excellent, didn't change much compared with its predecessor, the Apple Watch Series 10. Better heart rate tracking and new holistic health information are big pluses, and Audio Intelligence could potentially be a powerful new feature. It's a lot of new tech packed into a watch that sticks to the same base price as the model it replaces. Keep an eye here in the coming weeks for our full review of the Apple Watch Series 12.

item.title: Nintendo Isn't Getting Rid of Physical Games (Yet), But You Have to Watch Out for Game-Key Cards
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.02
Physical media's dying. Sony is dropping disk support in 2027. The physical version of Grand Theft Auto 6 will be a code-in-a-box. And it sounds like Xbox won't be supporting physical games for much longer. But what about Nintendo? While physical releases for the Switch 2 don't seem to be ending anytime soon, the company has its own controversial half measure: Game-key cards. If you're shopping for a new Switch 2 game, you need to be aware of game-key cards. You may already know that Nintendo's console supports regular game cards, where the game files are stored on the physical cartridge, but game-key cards are different, since they don't actually contain the full game data. It's confusing, for sure, but here's what you need to know before buying Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Resident Evil Requiem, or another big name game. What Is a Game-Key Card? As Nintendo explains, game-key cards are "your 'key' to downloading the full game to your system via the internet." They come in a case and include cartridges that slide into the Switch 2, just like any other physical release. However, you'll be shocked to learn that you need an internet connection to download the game's files before playing for the first time. It's worth noting that game-key cards don't need a continuous connection to play after the initial download, but the card does need to be inserted into the Switch 2. Additionally, these game cards aren't tied to a Nintendo account, so you can use them on other Switch 2 consoles or lend and resell your games. But the question remains: Are these truly physical games? Many have criticized Nintendo for devaluing physical media, leading the company to poll players about their feelings on the game-key card. I'm sure you're wondering why this even exists, right? Switch 2 cartridges top out at 64GB, but they're expensive for the publisher to use, so game-key cards will help get games into physical stores for a lot less money, Nintendo tells The Verge. However, this also means games like Puyo Puyo Tetris 2S—which is all of 4GB on Steam—are game-key cards because no one wants to pay more for storage they don't need. How to Tell If You're Buying a Game-Key Card Nintendo provides a helpful indicator on the box, but I needed to squint to read it. As illustrated in the image below, the case shows the game's rating in the bottom-left corner. Next to that is a key logo and the words GAME-KEY CARD. In very, very small print, it also says how many gigabytes of free space you need and a note: "Full game download via internet required." Crucially, there's a small key icon on the cartridge itself, which might not help you now but would be useful if you're looking to buy a used game without a case one day. While I think we've moved beyond the days when confused parents couldn't tell the difference between the Wii and Wii U, Nintendo notes the Switch 2 "supports both regular game cards and game-key cards," which I think still leaves some room for consumer confusion. If a publisher opts to use the game-key card format, there won't be a separate "true" physical release (at least not yet), but I fear folks might still grab a game off the shelf in Target only to get home and realize it's a game-key card. But does it matter? In the end, the game will still "be there," but if physical media matters to you, I can see this being a deal-breaker. Can you imagine buying a title before a long plane ride, only to realize the game won't load because you're not connected to Wi-Fi? If a game is on the cart, it can be theoretically played forever. If you need an internet connection to download the game, I worry what will happen when those servers go offline one day. Which Games Are Game-Key Cards? Many publishers have decided to use the game-key card format. This is allegedly because Nintendo only offered third-party developers the 64GB cartridge or the game-key card at launch—there was no smaller, standard physical cart. This would explain why nearly every major AAA release (and even some smaller games) is on a game-key card, since publishers don't want to pay extra for the more expensive storage space. Here's a list of games that are on a game-key card if you're trying to buy physical: Each of these games will require an internet connection to download before playing. It's also worth noting that titles like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Stage Tour, Civilization VII, Split Fiction, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4, and WWE 2K25 are actually only a code in a box. Even Nintendo is getting in on the act with Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension DLC. Bethesda's Fallout 4: Anniversary Edition and Skyrim Anniversary Edition were game-key cards, but Oblivion Remastered and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle received proper physical releases. Just be careful before buying online—I've seen at least one game show no Game-Key Card on one site, but feature it on another. Others are noticing as well, since "temporary" box art for pre-orders can lack the game-key card labels. I recommend checking multiple sites and reading through the product description to be sure. If you're truly dedicated to physical releases, one workaround I've seen discussed is buying the physical Switch 1 version and upgrading it to the "Switch 2 Edition" version after the fact. Nintendo seems to be banking on a lot of AAA releases heading to the Switch 2, including Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth and Elden Ring, both of which feature pretty hefty file sizes. That said, Cyberpunk 2077's devs managed to fit the game on a 64GB cart, and Bethesda switched to a true physical release for Oblivion after announcing it as a code in a box, so I think more physical releases can have the full game on the cart. It's also worth noting that smaller games are still vital to filling out Nintendo's catalog. To that end, 16GB and 32GB game cartridges have been rumored to exist since at least December, and Stellar Blade's Switch 2 release may be the first to explicitly mention a 32GB game card. If Nintendo has given publishers additional storage options, it might not mean that game-key cards are going away, but more options are a good thing, both for publishers and consumers. Given that PlayStation is dropping physical media, and Xbox isn't likely far behind, Nintendo's half-measure might soon be all we have. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% Review: Small Keyboard, Small Price, Big Value
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.61
You can't pigeon-hole Razer. Its gaming laptops are powerful, and esports athletes love its gaming keyboards and gaming mice for their performance-boosting features. I suppose if you were really trying, you could say Razer gear tends to be expensive. But even that's not necessarily true anymore, if you look at hardware like Razer's new Reclusa X Mini 65% keyboard, which is just $49.99. The Reclusa is not the fastest nor the most sensitive keyboard Razer has released—it’s firmly an enthusiast board, not a hardcore-gaming one. But it's also a mighty board for the money, with finger-pleasing key switches and customization features. To me, the best thing about the Reclusa is how many premium features it packs into its design while keeping the price low for any mechanical model. For that, it earns an Editors' Choice award as the best budget tenkeyless board you can buy. The Reclusa X Mini 65% is the first of a brand-new line of keyboards from Razer, denoted by “X” in the name, but it’s not the first time Razer’s used the Reclusa name. All the way back in 2007, Razer and Microsoft collaborated on the Microsoft Razer Reclusa, a distinctive oval full-size keyboard. But aside from the name, this new keyboard has no relation to the older board. It reminded me of the situation with the Karna Razer Boomslang, which was released in 1999 and then re-released as the Razer Boomslang in 2005 and again as an Anniversary Edition some months ago. (Karna, the company, was a predecessor to Razer itself, and Razer was a sub-brand of it.) The Reclusa, Razer claims, aims to deliver a rewarding experience right out of the box while also remaining open to future modifications. To that end, it uses the Razer Orange switch. Tactile and quiet, the Oranges are some of my favorite key switches, giving the Reclusa a luxurious typing feel with the stock switches. If these switches don't work for you, though, the Reclusa supports hot-swap compatibility for both three- and five-pin switches. The 65% keyboard's design is simple and clean. A small, black rectangle frame houses the five rows of keys. The body measures 1.5 by 12.4 by 4 inches and weighs 1.5 pounds. It's roughly the same size as the company's Huntsman V3 Pro Mini. It’s a sturdy device in hand, and thanks to its size, it takes up very little desk space, making it an ideal choice for cramped workspaces. I normally prefer a full-size keyboard, but the adjustment period wasn't as bad as I imagined. With only five rows of keys in the layout, additional functions such as volume control are subsumed into other keys as key combinations. Like its bigger, more expensive cousins, the Reclusa X Mini 65% incorporates silicone dampening within its frame. This reduces resonance and minimizes the hollow noise often associated with mechanical keyboards. By absorbing the excess vibration from key presses, the dampening layers produce a more consistent sound with every stroke, regardless of which switches are installed. In use, that sound translates to a clean, satisfying click. It’s not the quietest mechanical keyboard I've used (see the Be Quiet Light Mount for a recent example), but it’s quiet enough for shared office spaces and busy cafes. The keys have a travel distance of 3.5mm and an actuation force of 50 grams. (The actuation force is the minimum pressure required to register an input.) It's enough that those who spend most of their days typing will ease right into using the Reclusa, and casual gamers will find the resistance satisfying as well. Esports gamers may prefer lighter key actuation, but Razer has plenty of keyboards that cater to them. As far as its aesthetics are concerned, the Reclusa takes steps to differentiate itself from the typical black-and-white keyboards Razer usually traffics in. The keyboard features three-tone keycaps in white, black, and a light shade of green Razer calls Kelley Green. Textured double-shot ABS keycaps keep the letters and symbols on the keyboard legible over time, though I wish the keycap lettering were transparent, as it does suppress the RGB glow underneath. One subtle innovation Razer made that might excite the custom keyboard community is the change to so-called "south-facing" LEDs. With these, the LED is positioned below the switch mechanism, shining downward, as opposed to above ("north-facing") and shining straight up through the keycap. South-facing keys tend to emit more diffuse, even light, and sometimes, enable quieter operation since the LED isn't up in the keycap's movement zone. This aligns with the enthusiast-keycap standard used across the custom keyboard community, making the Reclusa compatible with a wider range of aftermarket keycaps. It's easy to see that the Reclusa is an impressive keyboard, but the more time I spent with it, the more I started to see what Razer trimmed to achieve that attractive $50 price. For one, the board has no feet to give it extra tilt. It doesn’t come with a wrist rest or a keycap puller, either. You won't find an OLED screen or a volume roller, and there are no 2.4GHz or Bluetooth wireless options; the small USB-C port at the top is the only way to connect it to your PC. These omissions don't bother me too much, though additional ergonomic options, like adjustable feet, are something Razer should consider as the line matures. Despite not being marketed as a gaming keyboard, the Reclusa X Mini 65% comes with a few gamer-focused features you might recognize from the Razer Huntsman V3. One returning favorite is Snap Tap mode, which is designed to help prevent instances where two opposing keys are pressed simultaneously. With the mode on, it’ll register the last input as the priority and keep you moving, a useful tactic in shooters and other action titles. You can also set what the keyboard prioritizes, too. If you’re keen to get granular in your keyboard’s settings, you can, for example, prioritize the depth of actuation between the two selected keys, so whichever key has a deeper depth of actuation will register first. In a similar vein, the Reclusa offers Dual Keypress Priority. During intense game sessions, you may occasionally press multiple directional keys, accidentally disrupting your own movement flow and control. Dual Keypress Priority manages that. For example, when holding A and W to move diagonally, pressing D will not override the current input. Only when A is released will the new directional input be registered. In addition to Snap Tap, Razer Snap Flex appears here. Snap Flex binds two keys to a single press, which allows both inputs to be executed together in a consistent, predictable manner. For example, if I wanted to prime a grenade in Call of Duty before I jumped and tossed it, I’d typically have to hold one button down, then the jump button, and then release the button. But with Snap Flex on, I can map the keyboard to both jump and release the grenade with a single button press. It might seem like a small adjustment, but it allows me to pull off that move every time. All these features and more are tweakable in Razer Synapse, Razer's downloadable utility. Here's where you can assign button functions, change RGB lighting effects, and more. My favorite feature is the key-switch-optimization option, which tweaks the switch sensitivity to better support you whether you're gaming or just typing. However, the Reclusa is not compatible with Razer's web app version of Synapse, so you'll have to download the software onto a Windows 11 computer to make use of the additional keyboard functions. While the Reclusa does have some features I wasn’t expecting, it’s not exactly the gaming keyboard for hardened esports players. It has a maximum polling rate of just 1,000Hz, for example. If you’re looking for a premium gaming keyboard, models such as the Corsair Vanguard Air 99 Wireless will be better suited for you. But I think enthusiasts or those new to keyboard customization and looking for a solid base to build on will find that the Reclusa is exactly what they’re after. For $50, the Reclusa is a great deal, and its out-of-the-box configuration is enough to impress even the pickiest of keyboard geeks. It’s a big improvement over the Razer BlackWidow V4 75% Barebones. And even if you don’t want to swap out any of Razer’s keycaps or switches, the gaming-forward features and strong RGB lighting will pair well with just about any casual gaming need. Final Thoughts Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% is an impressive addition to Razer’s keyboard portfolio. With the rising prices of computer goods, I was convinced that many would be priced out of keyboard customization as a hobby. But at $50, this is one of the best budget keyboards I've come across. If you’re looking to dabble in keyboard customization and don’t mind omissions like wireless connectivity, I wholeheartedly recommend the Reclusa X Mini 65% to start your experiments on. About Our Expert I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.
