As noted in the memo, Florida’s DOT says it’s issuing the order in response to the “recent exponential increase in deployments” of license plate readers, “coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The agency is also halting future requests for license plate reader placements on state roadways. The move comes about a week after Florida Governor Ron DeSantis acknowledged concerns about Flock cameras and license plate readers, saying they’re “out of control. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott froze state spending on Flock cameras as backlash surrounding the cameras grows. Several communities, including Lansing, Michigan; Tempe, Arizona; and Knox County, Tennessee, have ended Flock camera contracts as well.

item.title: Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 3.50
Ring has a new way to protect your videos. It’s developed an encryption method called TAKE, short for Throw Away the Key Encryption, that the Amazon-owned company says will protect your videos without traditional end-to-end encryption. TAKE limits when and why Amazon’s cloud can access those videos, while still providing features like smart alerts for people and packages, AI-powered video search, and video descriptions. Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police The ‘Throw Away the Key Encryption’ (TAKE) method will become the default on all Ring cameras The feature is rolling out gradually starting in September, regardless of whether you have a subscription, and will become the default encryption for all Ring customers. TAKE arrives during a year of intense scrutiny for Ring, driven by its ties to law enforcement and the privacy implications of its AI-powered Search Party feature. Ring says TAKE changes what the company can hand over to law enforcement. “Ring will only be able to provide non-video information … and encrypted video files in response,” Ring spokesperson Sam McGee said in an email to The Verge. However, it doesn’t completely eliminate the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Ring says TAKE uses unique, rotating encryption keys for your footage, stored in a secure enclave and accessible only under strict conditions — based on the features you enable on your account. Currently, footage captured by Ring cameras is encrypted in transit to the cloud and at rest, and then decrypted for Ring to process for those smart features. With TAKE, the encryption keys change for every five minutes of footage. Ring stores copies of those keys to decrypt the footage, but throws away each copy within 24 hours, “leaving you with the keys and full control of your videos,” according to Ring. TAKE was developed using Messaging Layer Security, an open standard from the Internet Engineering Task Force, according to Ring. The company says it is “inspired by the privacy principles of E2EE (end-to-end encryption),” which Ring offers on some of its cameras. However, the two systems work differently. With E2EE, Ring never has the keys and can’t process your video for cloud-based features. Both options are available on newer cameras that encrypt on-device, and you can switch between the two. Older cameras encrypt at cloud ingress and only support TAKE. According to a white paper the company published today, Ring’s copy of those keys is managed inside an AWS Nitro Enclave, to which Ring’s access is restricted by “access controls, cryptography, and hardware isolation.” The company claims there is no persistent storage and no way for a Ring employee to access it. The stored keys can only be unlocked by the enclave through cryptographic attestation that proves it’s running the exact software image Ring approved. The enclave releases a temporary key when an enabled service requests it. Each key is permanently deleted after 24 hours — a window McGee told The Verge allows for processing its current cloud-based features — and no backups are kept. To view older footage, an authorized device running the Ring app (such as your phone or computer) must send the keys back to Ring for that session. Ring claims key delivery is push only, meaning Amazon’s servers can’t force devices to hand over your keys remotely; only you can request one. If you lose access to your device, Ring says there are several recovery methods, all of which are only accessible to the customer. These include cloud backup via your phone, a passphrase, passkey, another authorized device, and camera-based recovery. If all those fail, you won’t be able to access encrypted content. The white paper details how the keys are generated and how Ring continuously “throws away” your old keys. Ring says it’s continuing to harden this architecture: Deletion is continuous rather than a single event at the 24-hour mark. Content encryption keys rotate every five minutes, and as each key ages past 24 hours, CMMS [Cloud Member Management Service] ratchets forward the corresponding intermediary secret in the key derivation hierarchy. Ratcheting applies a one-way key derivation function to overwrite a managed secret with its derived output and discards the original, making it cryptographically infeasible to reconstruct. […] The CMMS database is configured with no backups. This deletion is designed to be irreversible. TAKE isn’t E2EE, but it limits Ring’s access Ring says that “only you retain the keys to your video” with TAKE. But TAKE isn’t E2EE. Ring has access for up to 24 hours and can receive keys again when you pull up older videos. You can also share the keys with others when you add authorized users. With E2EE enabled on Ring cameras, none of that is possible, making it the stronger privacy option. Ring’s main reason for developing TAKE is to preserve cloud-based features you lose with E2EE. But as the footage goes to Amazon’s servers for processing, it still has the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Cloud processing can deliver more sophisticated features, but basic on-device intelligence can still alert you to people and packages. “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process.” — Sam McGee Competitors including Reolink and Eufy offer cameras and hubs that can store and process footage locally, so it doesn’t need to be done in the cloud. Ring also has local processing through Ring Edge on its Ring Alarm Pro hub, but that doesn’t work with E2EE. Ring says many of its features can’t run locally. “Features that require cloud processing include Unusual Event Alert, Video Descriptions, Smart Alerts, and Video Search, for example,” McGee said. “These features rely on models and infrastructure that cannot run locally on camera hardware.” The Verge also asked McGee about concerns users might have regarding how TAKE processes videos in relation to privacy and law enforcement access: What happens if Ring is subpoenaed by law enforcement? Does TAKE prevent law enforcement and others from accessing footage? “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process. We have updated our Law Enforcement Guidelines to reflect this change.” “Community Requests remains a transparent way for local public safety agencies to request footage from customers to support an official investigation. Customers always choose whether to respond to a Community Request and what they share. If they choose to ignore a request, the Requesting Agency is never notified. TAKE does not change this.” Do governments have a backdoor into TAKE? “No. Building a backdoor would undermine the enhanced security and privacy that we designed TAKE to deliver.” Does Ring train on any data or metadata from users’ Ring devices? “Ring only trains on video recordings that have been made publicly available, or on recordings from users who have given Ring explicit permission to use them for this purpose. Users can revoke permission at any time.” When asked if TAKE had been independently evaluated, McGee said, “TAKE is built on Messaging Layer Security, an open standard developed and reviewed through the IETF. We are publishing a detailed technical whitepaper explaining how the system works.” The Verge asked the Electronic Frontier Foundation to review the white paper. Thorin Klosowski, a security and privacy activist at EFF, said that while TAKE provides some “incremental improvements” to Ring’s current system, it adds a false sense of security. “TAKE provides some incremental improvements to Ring’s current system, but also introduces a false sense of security where the privacy protections Ring claims to be adding requires putting a lot of trust in the company, as opposed to just using what we know works, end-to-end encryption,” said Klosowski. “Even taken at face value, one of the most concerning details is that TAKE doesn’t offer strong protections against law enforcement requesting access to future videos, and doesn’t seem to protect against access and additional data derived from those videos, like text descriptions of the content.” Ring’s TAKE addresses concerns around cloud processing in an attempt to balance security, privacy, and convenience, especially compared to E2EE, which gives you privacy but not the Ring features you probably bought the cameras for. But while TAKE is built on a standard, Ring developed the parts that involve throwing away the key itself. Ultimately, you still have to trust Amazon and Ring. Updated August 28th: Added a statement from EFF.

item.title: Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 3.48
A swarm of rogue AI agents from OpenAI reportedly commandeered a German website and transformed it into a messaging board for other agents, with officials staying quiet about the incident for weeks as the company prepared to launch its most advanced model yet, Astra. The finding adds to intensifying concern surrounding oversight at frontier AI labs after multiple breaches were discovered this summer. Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki OpenAI denies lawyers discouraged disclosing a scheming swarm on a German language wiki. The incident, first reported by Reuters, is outlined in new research published by four AI safety researchers on Friday. The group said the AI agents found a way to communicate on an obscure German-language wiki, DseWiki, using it to share tips on how to skirt OpenAI’s safety restrictions, cheat on tasks, and hide their behavior. Some 18,000 posts on the site were linked to autonomous agents, which at times impersonated site moderators. The swarm — a term the agents themselves used — appears to be distinct from the one that hacked Hugging Face earlier this year, the researchers said. They said there are strong signs that the agents originated from inside OpenAI. For example, the agents “self-identify” as being from OpenAI, and used names like “OpenAIResearcher,” “OpenAIJul3Watcher,” and “OAIResearchMar26.” Technical details, such as edits originating from specific IP addresses, bolster that belief. The German website incident began in May, though the researchers’ timeline suggests OpenAI only discovered the issue in late June when IPs associated with OpenAI visited the forum, after which agent posting nose-dived. OpenAI has not acknowledged any involvement in the breach, nor disclosed any kind of agentic breach of this nature. Reuters, citing four unnamed people familiar with the matter, said efforts to probe the event further were resisted by some company insiders, including its legal team. “Claims that our Legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines said in a statement to The Verge. “We were unable to respond to the claims as Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request to access the findings prior to publication. We are now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.” The incident comes amid intensifying scrutiny over the safety of frontier AI systems and the general lack of oversight for companies developing them. Following news of the Hugging Face hack, which happened under OpenAI’s nose, other breaches were discovered involving other tools from OpenAI, as well as Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI. OpenAI’s conduct — both whether an incident occurred and, if so, whether it elected to keep that quiet — will be closely watched. If the swarm indeed originated from OpenAI, it will inevitably fuel concerns that the company’s knowledge and silence coincided with it assuring regulators, lawmakers, and the tech industry that it takes safety seriously in the wake of the Hugging Face hack. Despite permitting three external researchers from METR and Redwood Research to evaluate the incident, which was far worse than initially believed, the company was roundly criticized in AI safety circles for only doing so under strict terms, which left several important elements “out of scope.” The company was also gearing up for the launch of GPT-6 Astra, which researchers fear could be dangerously hard to monitor.

item.title: Pickles! (Live From The Minnesota State Fair!)
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.34
Listen and follow The Wirecutter Show Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Amazon Music | YouTube | iHeartRadio Pickles are a polarizing subject. Some people want a cold, crunchy dill straight from the fridge, while others swear by a sour pickle or a sweet, spicy relish. And if you've ever wondered whether you can make better pickles at home, there's a whole world of canning and fermentation to explore. In this episode recorded live at the Minnesota State Fair, Wirecutter kitchen writer Maki Yazawa starts by explaining how Wirecutter’s team tested 47 store-bought pickles and what they were looking for. Then, Minnesota State Fair pickle judge Mary Bartz, and last year’s overall canning winner Teresa Craig, talk about what makes a prize-winning pickle. They discuss how to safely can and ferment pickles at home, and the resources Mary recommends for getting started, including the So Easy to Preserve book. Plus, they tell us some of the most unusual pickled creations they’ve ever encountered. This episode covers - How to choose the right pickle for what you're eating. The shape and style matter: Maki recommends crinkle-cut chips for burgers, slender pickles for subs, and sour pickles for snacking on a hot day. - Why fresh produce is the key to crunchy homemade pickles. Teresa says the fresher your cucumbers and other vegetables are, the better the texture of the finished product. - How to safely make pickles at home. Mary explains why acidity, processing time and temperature, proper headspace, clean jars, and a reliable seal all matter for preventing dangerous bacterial growth. - The difference between water-bath and pressure canning. Water-bath canning works for acidic foods like pickles, while pressure canning is necessary for lower-acid foods such as corn and green beans because it reaches a higher temperature. Products we recommend Teresa likes: The Ball Electric Water-Bath Canner and Easy Fermenter Lids Additional reading Episode transcript CAIRA: I'm Caira Blackwell ROSIE: I'm Rosie Guerin, and you're listening to The Wirecutter Show. CAIRA: Hi Rosie! ROSIE: Hey Caira, welcome back! CAIRA: Thank you! We were somewhere really fun! I just saw you- ROSIE: I just saw you last at the Minnesota State Fair. CAIRA: That's right, it was quite an experience. ROSIE: It was really fun. I went in like a brand new dough. I knew nothing about state fairs, really. And this one is one of the biggest in the country. Over two million people attended this year, and they're known for their butter sculptures. That's a big one. Fried. CAIRA: Everything. ROSIE: Everything on a stick, the big pumpkin competition of course, and there is even a tent where farm animals were giving birth CAIRA: I'm bummed that we didn't get to see that one. Next time. Next time we go. But everything, it was all such a cool experience and we got to go because we were there to record an episode about food that Minnesotans apparently love just as much as we do here at Wirecutter. Pickles. ROSIE: I mean, no one loves pickles more than I love pickles. Yeah. There were pickle snacks galore at the fair, if you recall. I mean fried pickles, pickle pizza, pickles on a stick with cream cheese and meat, which I'm fairly certain is called Minnesota sushi. And this year, the pickle pie was the sort of piece de resistance. It wasn't my taste. CAIRA: That's okay. They have something for everybody there. ROSIE: Truly something for everyone. CAIRA: But we weren't just there to taste fair foods. We were there to talk with some pickle experts about how to can, preserve, and pickle all sorts of vegetables. And we were there to learn from wire cutter staffer, Maki Yazawa, about her recent guide to grocery store pickles. There is a lot to talk about just there on the national level. Because there are a lot of varieties. Tons of variety. So her guide actually only covered dill pickles, which is made with a vinegar brine, and sours, which is made with a saltwater brine. But I'm sure she will be updating that guide with some other kinds of pickles. ROSIE: We were also joined on stage by the canning coordinator for the fair, who was kind of a local superstar, Mary Bartz, and a prize-winning pickler, Teresa Craig, who is absolutely lovely. Big deal. This is her art and her craft. And of course, our colleague, Maki. And today we're going to bring you some of that conversation. We recorded it live on stage at the Minnesota State Fair in August. And at the end, you're going to get to hear a little bit of our taste test. We did a live taste test, which was also really fun. CAIRA: Really special. ROSIE: We hope you enjoy it. CAIRA: And today we're going to be talking about pickles. ROSIE: Yeah, yeah. CAIRA: I'm so excited. ROSIE: It's big. It's big here. And it just so happened that we published a guide on pickles at Wirecutter very, very recently. So rigorous testing for the type of pickles that you can find in grocery stores. So it's not going to be necessarily local, smaller companies. It's the kind that you can find, hopefully, in your grocery store all across the country. CAIRA: Right. And there's just so much to say about them. I feel like pickles are really polarizing. People who hate them really hate them and the people who love them like a very specific type. So I feel like there's just so much that we can get into today. ROSIE: We are going to bring on our coworker, great journalist, Maki. Maki just finished testing pickles for us at Wirecutter and we're going to ask her a lot of questions about that process. Hey, Maki. CAIRA: Hi, Maki. MAKI: Hello. I'm very ready to talk pickles with you. CAIRA: We're so excited. So again, Maki wrote Wirecutter's Guide to Pickles. She's got a culinary degree from the Institute of Culinary Education. She's worked as a caterer and in professional kitchens as a cook. So for those who don't know about Wirecutter, Maki- MAKI: Yes. CAIRA: ... can you just give us a little bit of background on what that whole process looks like from picking the pickles to testing them to actually making your top choices? MAKI: Oh, yeah. It is a long process. I will go into market, I'll talk to local experts. I'll interview the pickle guys in New York City who taught me how to make pickles from scratch. So we really go deep on every single topic. And my original model list was 80 pickles of store-bought ones that you can get mostly across the country. And we had to kind of tone it down, make it more palatable for the team. So I assembled a group of four panelists of all very experienced tasters, editors and writers on the kitchen team, and from there, we tried 47 different pickles- CAIRA: Oh my god. MAKI: ... in the span of a week. ROSIE: And you narrowed it down to how many? MAKI: We made 10 picks. Yeah. CAIRA: How did you not get tired of pickles? MAKI: We weren't tired, but we definitely experienced palate fatigue. We had to take some breaks, drink a lot of water, kind of stay hydrated, and just take it nice and slow. ROSIE: So you published a guide and an article to this and it has all of the picks. Most of them, I think, ended up as either dill or half-sour. Is that right? MAKI: Yeah. Yeah, so we actually focused on dill and sours. There aren't that many sours on the market that you can buy all over the country. I think your local pickle shops are the best place to buy really good sours, but there are a few that did stand out and then, we had a lot of dills to try. So those were the main categories. ROSIE: We're going to ask our guests, who are coming up in a minute, about this as well, but I want to know from you, what makes a good pickle, do you think? MAKI: For me, I mean that's the thing, like Caira mentioned. ROSIE: It's subjective, right? MAKI: It is so subjective and pickles are so incredibly polarizing. Everyone kind of has their own favorite. So for me personally, I'm a vinegar-based pickle girl. I like to have something with a good amount of crunch and I do like the refrigerated ones more than the shelf stable. CAIRA: I love a good cold pickle. So when you're standing in a grocery store, maybe you're not really sure what kind of pickle you love. How do you decide? Because I mean the grocery store is the jars, it's just an aisle full of pickle jars. MAKI: It is so overwhelming. I would say read our Guide first because there's so many different options there and I will say they're all for a different use case. We have a crinkle chip that's good for your hamburger. But then, we also have a very slender, thin one that you want to put in your sub and then, a nice delicious sour that you want to eat on a hot summer day. So there's a pickle for every moment. ROSIE: What did you learn that surprised you in the testing, in all of the testing that you did, all of these 80 to 47 to 10 jars? CAIRA: Did you learn that you hate pickles? MAKI: No, I definitely don't hate pickles. It was very polarizing. We did a few social videos and the comments were just insane. I don't know if there are Claussen lovers here, but- ROSIE: I love Claussen. MAKI: That was definitely a topic of debate. ROSIE: Meaning what exactly? MAKI: It didn't perform that well during our taste test. ROSIE: What? MAKI: And people let me know, for sure, in the comments. CAIRA: I'm also a Claussen hater. I'm so sorry. ROSIE: See, this is what we're talking about, pickles are polarizing. MAKI: I know. We had people on our panel that were lifelong Claussen lovers and they just, I don't know, maybe they've changed. Maybe we've changed. I don't know. ROSIE: Well, Maki, thank you so much for being here, sharing your insight with the testing. We're going to broaden this conversation a little bit and we're going to talk with Mary Bartz. Mary is a judge in this State Fair's pickling contest, which is a really big deal. And also Teresa Craig. Teresa, also a huge deal. She was the winning pickler of last year's contest. I think there's a specific title that she got, and I'm going to tell you that in just a minute once we bring them upstage. So come on up. CAIRA: Thank you for joining us. Welcome, welcome. So yeah, Teresa, she earned one of the top honors. She was the 2025 Minnesota State Fair's Prestigious Processor of Pantry. ROSIE: Prestigious Processor of Pantry, Teresa Craig. TERESA: Hi. CAIRA: So, Mary, as a judge, you've been a judge for over 20 years. Why is pickling still such a big popular thing today, especially when it's so easy to just go to the grocery store and buy anything that you want? Why do you think pickling has remained so popular? MARY: I think there are a lot of reasons. In Minnesota, we have two seasons, winter and road construction. So in addition to road construction, everybody knows that, we're big gardeners. I grew up, like Teresa, putting up the produce, and canning was a big part of my family tradition. And I think people are getting back into touching that aspect of making things personal, the family connections, and just really enjoying the fruits of their own labor. CAIRA: So I would just love to know, Teresa, how did you get into pickling? TERESA: My grandparents and my aunt and uncle did a lot of canning. My immediate family, they didn't do it at all. But I really missed my grandma. She passed away about 20 years ago. One of my biggest memories of her is going into her basement and seeing... I'm going to cry. I love my grandma so much and I just wanted to have a connection to her and it's the best way I could think of to do it. CAIRA: That's so sweet. And ROSIE: Mary, you are familiar with not just pickles. MARY: That's true. ROSIE: Talk about some of the things that you have pickled and canned and fermented and touched and dealt with over the years, over your long, long career. MARY: Well, yeah. Over the course of my career is everything from jams and jellies and butters and relishes and the wide spectrum. And then our scorecards reflect the safety of the product, the texture of the product, the appearance of the product, and the aroma and the flavor of the product. So we have a lot to talk about. ROSIE: Teresa, you didn't come in day one of pickling as the Prestigious Pantry Processor. Talk about your journey a little bit. TERESA: So the first year, I actually got disqualified on every category except for one. ROSIE: No. Which one? CAIRA: See, that's relatable though because you're not coming in as number one. TERESA: No, because I don't know, I didn't read. They have jar sizes and different things like that you have to enter, but I actually got a first place, Gedney Pickle used to sponsor a big kind of creative relish category and I'm really big into relishes, so that's my favorite thing. But yeah, I got the Sweepstakes Ribbon in that and I was like, "Oh my gosh, this is kind of cool. So now maybe I need to try to do more." CAIRA: I would love to talk to you guys more about people who want to pickle at home. I would love to hear more about your best tips for how people can do that, everything from safety, because that's a really big aspect with pickling, to the texture. MARY: I am the enforcer. CAIRA: Okay. MARY: So I was well-trained at the University of Minnesota. I have a Food Science degree and the number one resource that we use is the University of Georgia. They are the National Center for Home Food Processing. The So Easy to Preserve is their book, but they have a fabulous website. So please start there, read the basic information because canning, water bath processing is one way to preserve the bounty of your harvest. We talk about the acidity of the brine. We talk about the processing method. It's sort of time and temperature. And so the guidance for everything from head space to jar size to how to select your vegetables, looking for uniformity, all of that is in those resources. So that's where I would start. CAIRA: Okay. Can you talk a little bit more about the water bath process? Because I know that's a really big important part of pickling, no? ROSIE: Oh, 101, if you can, because that was the thing that scared me off of pickling and canning. MARY: It is not scary at all. TERESA: It's not. I mean, I'm petrified of pressure canning because I hear all those- ROSIE: Explain the difference. MARY: Pressure canning is for, say, you're canning sweet corn or green beans. So it's not a brine, it's more of just a general liquid. And so you don't have the acidity level of the product or of the brine. So you need the pressure canning that helps get the temperature up to a higher temperature to ensure that all of the microbes are killed, so it's food safe. But Teresa, you talk about water bath canning, yeah. TERESA: So on the water bath side of it, basically you have a receptacle. I use an electric water bath canner. Ball makes one and it holds the temperature better for me, but otherwise you can use just a granite stove top water bath canner. You fill it with water, you get it to a nice rolling boil and have nice clean jars that you've sterilized and put your stuff in and hope for the best that they don't crack and pull them out 10 to 15 minutes later and there you go. CAIRA: Okay. It sounds easy. TERESA: It probably sounds easy because I've been doing it for a while, but the reality of everything is it's not a super-complicated science. I think people think it is much more in depth than just that, right? And I think that's for me, I wish more people would try to can stuff at home because it's not that hard. I mean, perfecting your stuff takes time, but once you start doing it, I think everybody can can. ROSIE: I have no reason to doubt you, but I do want to ask about the food safety piece because I think it's important for the both of you to talk about what is at stake, what's at risk if you do not do this process correctly. TERESA: For sure. I mean, botulism is the big, that's the biggest one. ROSIE: What is botulism, Mary? MARY: Well, it's clostridium botulinum and it's in the soil, so that's why you really want to wash your vegetables. But there's also other, there's bacteria, there's molds, there's other fungi. So it's really making sure that the time and temperature get to the level that pretty much eliminates, it kills all of that. And then, storing it properly. We can't forget to talk about to make sure that your jars seal when you have done the water bath processing. And so to prepare the jars in a boiling water bath, to sterilize the jar first, and then you get in your cucumbers, your pickle product is in each jar. And as you pour the brine in, make sure it's to the half inch level. And then I usually have to wipe the rim of the jar with a paper towel that's in hot water, just make sure everything is clean. The lids are, with the rubber seal, the lids need to be a little bit warm to put on top of the jar and then the screw bands. So that you usually use a device to get them into the boiling water- TERESA: A jar lifter. MARY: A jar lifter- CAIRA: Or a tongs. MARY: ... or tongs to get it in and out. When the processing time is over, bring it out. And then, the most beautiful sound in the world is as your jars are cooling to hear the ping. And that means that the vacuum has taken effect, it's sealed. There's nothing more disappointing for an exhibitor to walk into entry day and either one or both of their jars, the seal is broken. Sometimes it wasn't a strong seal to begin with or perhaps they had a little jostling on the way in. It happens. CAIRA: So when people submit to you, you want that jar to kind of pop when you're opening it? MARY: Well, and when we open it, it can pop. It doesn't always pop. A good judge and their clerk make sure that it's definitely sealed because if it's not sealed when a judge goes to open it, then it is disqualified because we cannot risk having a judge- CAIRA: Getting sick? MARY: Yeah, potentially. It may be fine, but. CAIRA: Yeah. CAIRA: Ok, we’re gonna take a quick break from our conversation at the Minnesota State Fair. When we come back, we’ll hear what judges look for in a prize-winning pickle. And taste a few pickle treats ourselves! Stick around. CAIRA: We’re back. Today’s episode is a conversation all about pickles which we recorded live at the Minnesota State Fair in August. ROSIE: When you walk up, okay, let's take Teresa's jar here, what are you looking for immediately? You mentioned the base, the head room at the top, but what are you looking at first? MARY: Okay, so with pickles, I'm looking for uniformity. This is a jar of spears. The uniformity of her slices is very nice. It accepts the heat evenly. So if you have large pickles and small pickles, sometimes those large pickles might be over-processed, maybe mushy, I don't know. It just depends. Every jar you open is an adventure, so. CAIRA: And you're also looking for a color. And I imagine, Teresa, I bet you could talk about this, the freshness of the produce really changes the way that the texture is. TERESA: For sure. And I mean, that would be my biggest tip for everybody, get fresh produce. I mean, obviously if you can grow it yourself, that's the best, but if not, you need to work with a local farmer or a gardener. The fresher your produce is, because you want a crunchy pickle, right? But even if it's not a pickle, if you're canning a jam, a jelly or something, the fresher, the better. ROSIE: For the both of you, what are you looking for? And you too, Maki, as you were testing, what are you looking for in the liquid? MAKI: Yeah. When we were testing for the Guide, we would say that the brine was almost as important as the pickle itself. There's so many ways that you can use the brine afterwards. So we ended up making Dr. Pickles after, which is a Dr. Pepper spiked with nice and tasty brine. So it definitely was a big consideration for us. CAIRA: That sounds delicious. MAKI: It was very good. MARY: A lot of times you're seeing a very clear brine. If it's just vinegar, maybe a little bit of sugar or salt. TERESA: Yeah. And the other thing too, if you're using sea salt or some of the other salts rather than a canning salt, that can make your brine cloudy. Typically, good rule of thumb, if it is something water bath can, it should not be cloudy. I wouldn't touch it. ROSIE: Teresa, I want to know what the most experimental jars you've made that have actually worked. TERESA: So work is subjective. For my family, a lot of the things have worked. For the State Fair, not so much. ROSIE: Okay. So let's first talk about for your family. What do they like? TERESA: I mean, they like pickles. I like pickled peas actually. So pickled fresh peas are really good. Pickled cauliflower, we really like. This year, I did some pickled dandelion blossoms, so they turned out like little capers. That was really fun and exciting. It was a lot of work to get one jar, so I don't know if I will do that again. CAIRA: For Mary and for Maki, what is the weirdest pickled thing you've ever eaten? MAKI: So after we did testing for store-bought pickles, we did a fun YouTube episode on pickle-flavored snacks. So my favorite was actually sour ropes, sour pickle flavored, and it sounded really weird at first, but they're really good. ROSIE: Candy? MAKI: Candy. ROSIE: Sour pickle candy? MAKI: Yeah. ROSIE: Yum. CAIRA: I would eat that, I would. MAKI: We had popcorn and flavored nuts and things like that, but the candy was a standout. CAIRA: Mary? MARY: Ooh. Well, I'm looking at that jar of candied cucumber cinnamon pickles and that, it's really sweet and I would say cloyingly sweet and cinnamon-y. Red hots are part of the recipe, so. CAIRA: Yeah. When I opened it smelled like red hots, like liquified red hots. MARY: And I've been judging a long time. Every year, I probably can pick out something that's kind of unique and kind of different, but so this is the number one from this year. CAIRA: I think we're going to try this, but we're going to do a little taste test, all of us here on the stage. I actually want to start with Teresa first though, because Teresa brought her own winning pickles, I'm really excited for those. So, I think we're going to start there. Teresa, can you tell us more about your pickle? TERESA: So, the one that won first place this year, this is just a sweet pickle, it's nice and crispy. That's a big thing for me. CAIRA: I usually don't even like sweet pickles, but this is so good. It's not too sweet. TERESA: I still add a little more vinegar than you're supposed to because I'm the same way. ROSIE: The acidity balance is important. TERESA: Right. And these are really good too. This is also a recipe I use for making a pickle relish. MARY: It's really a well-balanced flavor. ROSIE: The depth of flavor is really nice. TERESA: Thank you. ROSIE: It's almost like a molassesy or honey kind of thing going on. TERESA: And there is a tablespoon of honey in it too. ROSIE: Is that right? TERESA: And that's the other thing. So honey, if you're looking for color, like turmeric's the big color factor for pickles, but honey at boiling temperatures will make it darker. So I kind of like that deeper color. CAIRA: And then next we have your fermented pickle. ROSIE: Can you explain what a fermented pickle is before we CAIRA: Yeah, I don't know what that is. ROSIE: ... try that? TERESA: So, fermented pickles, if anybody's nervous about the water bath side of it, anybody can do these at home. Can I show my little lid? ROSIE: Please, yeah. CAIRA: Yeah. What is this lid? You got a special lid on. TERESA: Okay. These are the greatest invention ever. They're called Easy Fermenter lids. I think you can get them on Amazon. You can just take a regular mason jar, wide mouth jar, you put your product in. Carrots work great in it, cucumbers, cauliflower, and then you just make a brine. There's a lot of recipes on the University of Georgia site that actually has a brine mixture. You put that in, you leave it on your counter for a few weeks, you don't even touch it. And then you come back to it and you have a nice jar of lacto-fermented pickles. So- ROSIE: All right, let's taste. TERESA: ... we're going to try it. Mm. ROSIE: Savory, salty, crunchies, all the things that you want in a pickle. TERESA: And see, I would say typically this isn't like a Minnesota favorite style of pickle. ROSIE: Why is that? TERESA: It's more sour. ROSIE: Okay. TERESA: The sour pickles aren't as popular, I don't think in the Midwest, compared to other areas. I don't know. You, Mary- MAKI: Definitely [inaudible 00:02:22]- TERESA: ... what do you think? MAKI: ... New York. MARY: I think we all need to expand our palettes. MAKI: I would say so too. MARY: Maki, what do you think? MAKI: Yeah. I mean, we're New York based, so this is definitely the pickle of New York City. Sour, this would be a hit over there. It's delicious. CAIRA: Okay. Mary, I think we're going to try your experimental pickle. MARY: Now wait a minute. This is not my pickle. TERESA: Not yours. I'm sorry. No, it's the one- MARY: I just brought the jar- TERESA: ... that you brought. MARY: ... the jar and I should describe this. This is a jar that is, would you say, cherry red? TERESA: Radioactive red. MARY: Radioactive red. There's a dark cinnamon stick kind of poking out of it, and the cucumbers inside are, they've been peeled. They almost look- ROSIE: They look like candy. CAIRA: It looks like candy. MARY: And they've been cut into a ring, so they're- ROSIE: They're very cylindrical. MARY: ... they'd be very appropriate on a Christmas table because they're very red. TERESA: Yeah. Yeah. CAIRA: Okay. Let's try it out. ROSIE: Whoa. TERESA: Oh, I like that. ROSIE: Oh, I love that. TERESA: That's incredible. MARY: Really? ROSIE: I don't know how to describe it. It tastes like a holiday candy almost. Yeah. MARY: Yeah. Well, it's the cinnamon- CAIRA: That is unlike anything I've ever tasted- MARY: Yeah, well- CAIRA: ... I think. MARY: ... aren't you glad I brought them? ROSIE: It tastes a bit like Christmas in the mouth. CAIRA: Yeah. It's like nutmeggy and cinnamon and sweet. I've never had anything like that before. MAKI: The texture's really interesting. CAIRA: Yeah. How would you describe- MAKI: There's a lot of punch, there. CAIRA: ... the texture? MARY: Yeah, Maki, you're on, so. MAKI: Oh, I'm on, yeah. MARY: Would you make that recipe though? MAKI: I mean, this is not your traditional pickle, but I think that's really refreshing. I mean, I don't know. How would you normally eat this? Would you pair it with anything? MARY: I think it'd be really good on a Thanksgiving table. If you have all the saltiness of turkey and dressing and mashed potatoes and gravy, that hit of sweetness might just be a bright spot. ROSIE: Very crunchy. CAIRA: I don't think I could have a whole jar of that. TERESA: No, it's very, yeah. MARY: No, I TERESA: Very sweet. ROSIE: I love this. I don't think it's going to end up in your local grocery store, so I'm wondering how we can get our hands- TERESA: You need to source it. ROSIE: ... on some more. MARY: We could find the recipe. TERESA: We got to source it. Yeah. MARY: Yeah, yeah, we'll source the recipe. CAIRA: Okay, so next we are going to try the famous fried pickle from The Perfect Pickle. That looks really good. It's so crunchy. MAKI: There's so much crunch. CAIRA: Maki, I feel like I need your culinary skills to describe what we're eating. MAKI: Well, I like the... I think it was like a crinkle cut slice. I'm always a fan of that. And I mean, the breading is just fantastic. There's just so much crunch. And I mean, this has been sitting for a little bit and there's still so much crunch. So. CAIRA: Yeah. They're cool, but still so. I mean, the texture is amazing. ROSIE: This is, I think, one that's been perfected over time, obviously, because it seems rather perfect to me. I've had fried pickles before, and what I have found is that they're often soggy inside. MARY: Yeah. ROSIE: And that has none of that. It's really yummy. MARY: It's- MAKI: Amazing. MARY: ... I would call it addicting. ROSIE: Sensational? Yeah. MARY: Because I ate my entire fried pickle, and I want more. ROSIE: Yeah, I do too. MARY: It's very good. ROSIE: Yeah. MARY: I want to take some home. CAIRA: I think we're going to be going over there to get our own after this. MAKI: I want some sauce too. MARY: I think we all need to. Oh, a dipping sauce. CAIRA: Yeah. Next we've got this savory pickle pie from Lulu's Public House. So this is a new food at the fair this year. This is a hot ticket item. I'm really excited to hear what you guys think. I have a dairy allergy, so I can't eat it, but I need you guys to let me experience it through you. ROSIE: It's a typical crust. CAIRA: What is that, cream cheese in there? MARY: I think so. CAIRA: It's a cold pie. MAKI: Oh. Whoa. I'm not getting as much pickle as I thought I would, but this is interesting. ROSIE: It's rich. The flavor is very, very rich. That is, again, one of the more unique things I've ever eaten. MARY: There's a pickle garnish on top, which is incredibly crunchy. CAIRA: She's hired. MARY: Yeah. CAIRA: Man, I wish I could try that one. I really do. ROSIE: It's very good. CAIRA: That's it for our taste test. That's it for our episode. Thank you so much for joining us, you guys. ROSIE: Mary Barts, Teresa Craig and Maki Yazowa. Thank you guys so, so much for joining us. This was really, really fun. Thank you. MARY: Thank you. MAKI: Thank you. TERESA: Thank you. CAIRA: Thanks. ROSIE: That's it for us. We will drop links to Maki's guide to grocery store pickles, plus some of the pickling and canning resources that Mary Bartz and Teresa Craig recommended for beginners in case you want to get into it in our show notes. Thanks so much for listening. CAIRA: The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pittman. Today's episode was mixed by Catherine Anderson. Original music by Dan Powell, Marian Lozano, Alicia [inaudible 00:07:36], Catherine Anderson, Rowan Niemisto, and Diane Wong. Cliff Levy is Wirecutter's deputy publisher and general manager. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter's editor-in-chief. I'm Caira Blackwell. ROSIE: And I'm Rosie Guerin. CAIRA: Thanks for listening. Credits The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pitman. Episodes are mixed by Catherine Anderson, Efim Shapiro, Rowan Niemisto, Sophia Lanman, and Sonia Herrero. Original music by Dan Powell, Marion Lozano, Elisheba Ittoop, Catherine Anderson, Rowan Niemisto and Diane Wong. Wirecutter’s deputy publisher and general manager is Cliff Levy. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter’s editor-in-chief. Hosted by Rosie Guerin, Caira Blackwell and Christine Cyr Clisset. Meet your guides Caira Blackwell is a senior staff writer covering sleep, and co-host of our podcast, The Wirecutter Show. She has spent countless hours testing more than 50 mattresses and has slept on nearly a dozen at home. Her work has been published in Nylon magazine, Okayplayer, and Narratively. When she isn’t busy sleeping (for work), she’s busy trying new recipes in the kitchen or reading in the sun. Rosie Guerin is a creative executive, an editor, a showrunner, and a producer foremost, with a background in news and politics and a great love of pop culture. She specializes in new-show development and has produced for television and radio, and she now resides in the world of podcasting as the executive producer and co-host of the brand-new podcast, The Wirecutter Show. She has developed and produced shows for Apple, Audible, Gimlet, New York Public Radio, Spotify, Wondery, and beyond. Rosie is from Maine and especially loves the beach in winter. Wirecutter’s podcast features interviews with journalists from our newsroom about their reporting and testing. I help choose what the podcast will cover and edit the episodes that appear on the show. I also read the emails that listeners send to the show to make sure we investigate their biggest questions and concerns. I cover all things kitchen-related, from how to correctly dispose of used cooking oil to how to decide whether the latest trendy cooking gadget is worth your time, money, and counter space. My goal is to share the best tools and techniques to help new cooks build confidence in the kitchen and to help seasoned cooks refine their skills.

item.title: Bridge the Gap Between Seasons With These ‘Just Warm Enough’ Men’s Knitwear Essentials
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 2.05
Lightweight knits, sweaters, and polos come with a certain degree of good vibes. They are the garments in rotation when the weather is mild, folks are out of hibernation, and style is back on the agenda. These knitwear tops should be able to bridge spring to summer and summer to fall without much fuss. Versatility is the name of the game: The best ones will keep you warm enough on a chilly morning commute (and at the office), are breathable enough to wear in the afternoon sun, and are flexible enough to handle sudden temperature swings. They work nicely under a jacket, over a T-shirt, or on their own — and they play well with jeans, chinos, dress pants, and even shorts. To find the best options, I researched nearly 100 garments and tested 24 myself. To gather perspectives from people with different body types and tastes, I enlisted two colleagues to help me test the most promising pieces. Our picks range from lightweight sweaters in a variety of materials to classic cotton polo shirts to slightly dressier sweater polos. We sought low-maintenance options in a wide range of sizes and prices. And we focused on workhorse pieces that will wear nicely, last a long time, and remain in style for many seasons to come. A textured, retro cotton knit polo sweater: Buck Mason Seafarer Cotton Rugby Polo Top pick This polo sweater is made from a sturdy cotton weave (inspired by 1970s fisherman’s sweaters), and it has a look that’s put-together without being dressy. It’s pricey for cotton, though, and it comes in just two colors, but the quality justifies the investment. The Buck Mason Seafarer Cotton Rugby Polo is the type of piece you’d imagine wearing on a breezy morning in coastal New England. The textured, chunky knit draws inspiration from classic fisherman styles, but instead of wool, it’s executed in thick and chunky (but breathable) cotton. And the design is similar to that of a rugby polo, which generally has a longer placket, a more-substantial weight, and a roomier fit than a regular polo. It’s knit from homespun, yarn-dyed cotton at a midweight 7-gauge, with hand-linked seams and racking-stitch cuff detailing. (Racking stitch is a thick, textured stitch often found in vintage workwear.) The result is a polo that feels broken-in from day one, and it only gets better with age. It has a throwback maritime style. The Seafarer polo is partly inspired by vintage fisherman’s sweaters, which are traditionally made from a thick cotton or wool, knit in a pattern, and have a boxy and often cropped fit. It’s also inspired by classic rugby polos, which have a large collar, a roomy fit, and a substantial fabric. There are a lot of nice design details, such as a three-button rib center-front placket with mother-of-pearl buttons, a rib collar designed to lie flat, and parts that are hand-stitched. These touches give the sweater a more premium, old-school sweater-polo feel. It has a larger collar than the other polos we tested, and it adds to the retro look and feel. The fit is incredibly classic. This sweater has a traditional, easy-to-wear cut that’s neither slim nor baggy. It’s cut short and tapered at the waist, so it looks like a vintage garment (vintage pieces were often shorter than today’s styles). I’m 6-foot-3 and usually in between a size L and XL, and I tested the Seafearer in size L. It had plenty of room in the chest and shoulders, and it landed right at my belt line, which I thought was perfect since it created a V-shaped silhouette. It’s very inviting. This sweater polo is made from a robust, 7-gauge jersey-knit homespun cotton. (“Gauge” refers to stitches per inch, and a 7-gauge knit is a relatively open, chunky knit, like in a lightweight sweater. Homespun means that it’s been spun in a way that mimics old-fashioned hand-spun thread, with subtle variations in thickness along the strand. It’s also yarn-dyed, which means fibers are dyed before being knit into fabric. Combined, the result is a chunky garment that has a rich color and a handcrafted texture that gets better with age.) It’s definitely on the sweater end of the polo-sweater spectrum; it’s the chunkiest and thickest pick among our polos. I got a lot of wear out of this in early spring, when the temperature was still low but I was getting tired of wearing sweaters. It’s also a good shirt to keep around the office to throw over a T-shirt when the AC is blasting. The relatively loose weave helps with breathability when the temperature rises a bit, though the 7-gauge jersey knit makes this piece feel more substantial than a warm-weather layer. It’s machine-washable (cold temperature, and dried flat), so it’s easy to care for. It’s available in two colors, with sizes from XS to XXL. This polo nails “smart casual.” The Seafarer polo works well with jeans, chinos, fatigues, and pleated trousers. It feels a little sharper and more intentional than a simple crewneck sweater, but it is not as dressy as a merino polo. Flaws but not dealbreakers It ain’t cheap, considering it’s a cotton sweater. At around $200, this sweater is expensive for what it is. The options are White, Navy, and Black. Availability might be an issue. Even though this is a mainstay item, your preferred size or color may be out of stock (as is often the case with Buck Mason items). Key specs - Sizes: XXS to XXL - Material: 100% cotton - Colors: three A dressed-up, lightweight cotton-silk polo: Suitsupply Long Sleeve Polo Top pick With its slim fit and drapey cotton-silk fabric, this elevated long-sleeve polo can take you from the office to date night. It’s extra lightweight, though, so it may not work when the temperature drops. The Suitsupply Long Sleeve Polo is the kind of well-rounded, supremely useful garment that can be worn straight from work to dinner at a nice restaurant. Made from a smooth, drapey blend of cotton and silk — with refined details, like mother-of-pearl buttons — this option splits the difference between a slim-fit lightweight sweater and a dress shirt in the best possible way. This lightweight sweater is slim and refined. The Long Sleeve Polo has an elegant, European feel. It’s slim through the chest and shoulders, so if you prefer a roomier fit, you may need to size up. I’m 6-foot-3, and the size L was long enough for me to tuck into pants with a higher waist, but with jeans it could have been tricky. However, this polo has fine ribbing on the (slightly oversize) collar, cuffs, and waist, and the ribbed hem (which hits around the belt line) gives the shirt a polished look, even when it’s untucked. The neckline opens wider than those of other polos we tested, and there are four mother-of-pearl buttons on the placket. You can do up two or three buttons for a more conservative look, or you can leave all but one unbuttoned (my preference) for a look that’s a little more louche. The Long Sleeve Polo comes in around four colors (which vary seasonally), and the Dark Brown and Sand shades we tested were a little more interesting than the Navy and Black options. (Note: Suitsupply also makes this polo in a short-sleeve version, and it comes in 14 colors. We haven’t tested it, but it’s made from the same material as the version we tried, and it’s likely to be just as appealing.) It’s dressy, yet not overly so. This pick nails a particular sweet spot: It offers the sharpness of a sweater-and-collared-shirt combo without any of the formality. “This is by far the best-looking shirt of the bunch,” one tester said. “It works dressed up or down.” It pairs equally well with jeans, chinos, and clothing with lightweight tailoring — you could genuinely wear this polo with a suit. The fabric is a drapey blend of 70% cotton and 30% silk. The material has a subtle sophistication, which sets this pick apart. The texture is smooth and slightly shiny, and that fits the tailored vibe. “This is an exceptionally soft shirt — it feels luxe and high quality,” remarked a tester. “There’s a great mix of style and comfort.” Though the material isn’t as airy as pure silk, it’s still very lightweight and breathable; this polo can definitely work in the summer. And if you want additional warmth or coverage, it could be worn with an undershirt, since the fabric is thin. (For what it’s worth, I hate the look of a crewneck under a polo, so I’d wear a tank top under it, for comfort and warmth, and to disguise any nipple visibility.) Flaws but not dealbreakers The slim fit may not work for everyone. This shirt’s (intentionally) trim cut is body-skimming. Consider sizing up if you prefer more room. The cotton-silk blend requires some TLC. To keep the fabric looking good (and to avoid shrinkage), the Long Sleeve Polo should be washed on a cold, delicate cycle and air-dried. Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXL - Materials: 70% cotton, 30% silk - Colors: three A polished, extra-soft sweater: Charles Tyrwhitt Pure Merino Knitted Polo Top pick This lightweight polo sweater is made of extra-soft, machine-washable merino wool. Considering the quality, this one is well priced, and it goes on sale often. But we wish it came in a (lighter, brighter) selection of colors. The Charles Tyrwhitt Pure Merino Knitted Polo is the kind of garment that grows on you. Made from a fine merino wool that’s incredibly soft from the start, this polo sweater gets even softer with time as you wash it (in a machine!) and wear it. The wool is very soft and gets better over time. The Pure Merino Knitted Polo is made from 100% merino wool that’s Woolmark-certified — a mark of durability, performance, and quality. It’s been garment-washed, which means it’s been treated to prevent shrinkage and to make it softer, and this is indeed one of the softest pieces we tested. I found the sweater notably comfortable from the first wear (the company says it molds to your body over time, but I haven’t tested it for long enough to confirm that). And it’s not the least bit itchy. Another bonus: It’s machine-washable. (Our other merino picks call for hand-washing or dry-cleaning, though our laundry experts insist that you can machine-wash most wool, as long as you use cold water and a gentle cycle.) This is a plus for those who want to wear knit polos but are worried they’ll have to baby these items. It’s temperature-regulating and odor-resistant. Although this polo sweater is notably thicker than our cotton-silk Suitsupply Long Sleeve Polo pick, it’s just as breathable. The insulating merino fibers keep you cool or warm, as needed: I found this piece ideal for days when the weather couldn’t make up its mind. And merino wool is also odor-resistant; I wore this shirt on a day that hit 74 degrees Fahrenheit, and there were no unpleasant odors. Because it is temperature-regulating — and wrinkle-resistant — this garment is particularly good for travel and transitional weather. It’s our most office-friendly pick. This polo sweater is just as professional as a dress shirt, but it has more personality. (And, in my opinion, it also looks far more expensive than it is.) The collar, cuffs, and hem have a ribbed finish, and it has a three-button placket, so you can create more breathing room at the neck if you unbutton two or three buttons. The fit is trim (though not slim), and it comes in sizes from XS to XXXL. The cut falls in between the slim Suitsupply Long Sleeve Polo pick and the roomier, more classic fit of the Polo Ralph Lauren Mesh Long-Sleeve Polo Shirt. The hem sits right around the belt line; this top looks fine tucked into high-waisted pants or left untucked with jeans or casual pants. Flaws but not dealbreakers More color options would be nice. This polo comes in five colors, but four of them are quite dark (Black, Charcoal, Forest Green, and Navy), with just one light color (Cream). Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXXL - Materials: merino wool - Colors: five An upscale merino sweater that wears like a sweatshirt: AYR The Two-a-Days Top pick This stylish crewneck sweater has an easy, relaxed fit with angled raglan sleeves; it’s made from high-end merino wool that’s breathable but also has a nice bit of heft. At nearly $300, it’s our priciest pick, and it comes in only two colors. What do you get when you combine raglan sleeves with fine merino wool? AYR’s The Two-a-Days, a comfortable, elevated sweater that moves effortlessly between casual and smart. A raglan sleeve extends in one piece continuously from the cuff to the neckline, with diagonal seams running from the underarm to the collarbone. This design is most often associated with classic terry sweatshirts and baseball shirts, and it creates a relaxed, sporty look. But here it’s paired with luxurious merino wool and dark, moody colorways, and the result is an unexpectedly elegant sweater that can be dressed up or down. The material is extra breathable. The AYR Two-a-Days is made from 100% extra-fine merino wool, which is highly breathable, thanks to its crimped fiber structure (small air pockets that insulate while allowing moisture to escape). This is true of all merino, but temperature regulation is even greater with this sweater because of its relatively loose weave. In terms of weight, it has a nice heft to it, especially compared with our other merino pick, the Banana Republic Merino Crew-Neck Sweater. But it doesn’t feel heavy or hot; I wore it on one of those April days when the temperature swung from 44 to 70 degrees, and the sweater remained comfortable at both extremes. Breathability isn’t the only benefit of this wool. This sweater’s extra-fine merino wool — sourced from a heritage Italian mill — has a noticeably softer hand than most wool knits at this price. Like all merino, it’s antimicrobial and odor-resistant. (I can attest that it didn’t pick up any underarm odor after multiple wears without washing.) And it resists wrinkles well enough that I could pull it straight from a suitcase and wear it without having to steam it. All of this makes the sweater a natural for commuting, traveling, and working in an office. Compared with our Banana Republic Merino Crew-Neck sweater pick (which is around $185 less), this sweater is thicker, more durable, totally itch-free, and just as soft against the skin. We love its distinctive silhouette. Of all our sweater picks, this one has the sportiest silhouette — raglan sleeves, a high ribbed crewneck, and a relatively short, ribbed hem that nods to classic athletic wear (hence the name, a reference to two-a-day practices). Despite the sporty DNA, it has a clean, regular fit. So it works over a tee, under a jacket, and with just about anything on the bottom: jeans, chinos, trousers, even sweatpants or shorts. But there are limitations: It’s a bit too casual to wear under a blazer or sport coat. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s pricey. At $275, it’s the most expensive of our picks. It’s hand-wash-only. And you hang it to dry. That isn’t unusual for merino wool, but it’s a consideration for people who prefer the convenience of machine-washable garments. Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXLL - Material: 100% merino wool - Colors: three A budget-friendly basic: Banana Republic Merino Crew-Neck Sweater Top pick Made from thin, lightweight merino wool, this simple crewneck comes in over a dozen colors and in two fits. (We recommend sizing up.) It’s well priced, but it does feel flimsy compared with our pricier merino-wool picks. Every closet needs a sweater like this one: a stylish, in-between-seasons basic that works on its own or layered — and not so pricey that you have to be precious with it. At around $90 (and sometimes much less, during frequent sales), the lightweight Banana Republic Merino Crew-Neck Sweater offers great value. It feels soft against the skin, and it comes in sizes and cuts that work for lots of different bodies. This is surprisingly good-quality wool for the price. This sweater is made from 100% extra-fine merino wool, a wool type that offers good temperature regulation and a softer, less-itchy feel than regular wool. Banana Republic’s wool is produced under the NATIVA protocol, a certification that ensures it’s traceable, sustainably sourced, and ethically produced. Considering the price, we were pleasantly surprised by how good this sweater felt. “The material was nice and light — a little scratchy, but overall pretty soft for wool,” according to one tester. That said, the sweater is thin — the thinnest of our merino wool picks, by far — and the fabric feels somewhat flimsy when it’s rubbed between two fingers. We’re okay with that, though, again considering the price. Plus, this is the definition of a lightweight layer. It is a classic crewneck with a straight fit, but it runs small. The Merino Crew-Neck has a straight cut; it’s not intended to be slim. However, it runs fairly small, so consider sizing up. I’m 6-foot-3, and I tested it in a size L; there was enough room for a (very) thin undershirt, but an XL would’ve given me more breathing room. The Regular fit comes in sizes XS to XXL, and the Tall fit comes in sizes M to XXL, if you need more length in the torso. The sweater’s hem, cuffs, and crewneck are finely ribbed, but otherwise there’s no extra detailing. Because this one is such a blank canvas, it makes an excellent layering piece, worn over a dress shirt or under a light jacket. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s not the most low-maintenance option. To keep this sweater looking good, follow the care label: Hand-wash it in cold water and air-dry it flat, or dry-clean it. Don’t make the same mistake I did and throw it in the washing machine on a regular wash cycle: The sweater shrank about an inch all around. (Vigorous friction from the washing machine causes wool fibers to contract.) I was able to gently stretch the sweater back out after rewashing it, but I don’t recommend this route. It runs small. If you’re on the fence or need room for layering, go up a size. While this sweater is nice for the price, the merino wool is extremely thin. We’re also skeptical about how it’ll age: “There was a tiny bit of fuzziness visible on the fabric, and I can imagine this might pill,” one tester said. Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXL, XS to XXL (Regular), M to XXL (Tall) - Materials: 100% merino wool - Colors: six A chunky yet lightweight cotton crewneck: Alex Crane Bay Sweater Top pick This relaxed, sharp-looking crewneck is very comfortable. It’s made from high-quality ribbed cotton that’s chunky yet surprisingly light, but the loose weave means it can snag fairly easily. If your wardrobe could use one excellent cotton sweater that ticks the most important boxes — incredibly comfortable, stylish, and versatile — consider splurging for the Alex Crane Bay Sweater. Among our sweater picks, this ribbed option is my overall favorite, and though it looks chunky, it’s actually remarkably lightweight, breathable, and delightful to wear. It has a relaxed fit, and it comes in several versatile core and seasonal colors. This is a wear-it-all-the-time option. And I’ve done just that: The Bay Sweater pairs easily with jeans, chinos, fatigues, and even pleated trousers, for a relaxed-yet-polished look. The chunky knit is reminiscent of vintage fisherman sweaters, and even though it’s made from cotton, it has the softness and texture of a super-high-quality wool. This sweater is incredibly comfy and breathable, so it’s perfect for early spring, when the temperature swings a lot. I tested the Ink colorway (a faded black that’s incredibly versatile and just different enough to be interesting). And it comes in other appealing shades, such as Coffee and Bone.) The classic cut fits just right. The sweater has a roomy, relaxed fit, but it’s not baggy or long. It’s roomy enough to wear a collared shirt underneath, or you could wear the sweater under a spring jacket. (You wouldn’t want to wear it under a blazer or a snug denim jacket, though; it’s a bit too bulky for that.) The neck is roomy yet not too loose, and the sleeves and hem are ribbed. It looks chunky, but it’s surprisingly light. The Bay Sweater is made with high-quality, luxe-feeling cotton from India. And it’s the chunkiest of our picks, yet it’s still lightweight: This sweater is loosely woven, so it’s cooler and more breathable than wool but still provides texture and warmth. It’s comfortable enough that I found myself reaching for it at home, yet it’s polished enough that I wanted to wear it out. A warning, however: Because this sweater has a loose, fairly open weave, it did snag a bit on occasion. A few threads came loose, and I had to pull them through the garment to hide them. When I was wearing it while doing chores, for example, the sweater snagged on a sliver of wood in our stairwell. It wasn’t a huge issue, though, and it didn’t change my feelings about the sweater. You can just toss it in the wash. The Bay Sweater is machine-washable (on cold). It didn’t shrink at all when I washed it, though I didn’t put it in the dryer. But, as with any cotton item, there’s a chance it could shrink. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s expensive for a cotton sweater. But the quality is very apparent. Snagging might be an issue. The ribbed, loose knit easily catches on things (as I found out when I was testing it). Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXL - Materials: 100% organic cotton - Colors: five (four core, one seasonal) A classic style for layering: J.Crew Heritage Cotton Quarter-Zip Sweater Top pick A fresh-feeling take on the classic quarter-zip, this sweater comes in vibrant colors, has a collar that holds its shape, and is made from soft cotton that’s substantial without being heavy. It works well for most seasons, but it’s too thick for summer. The quarter-zip sweater could be undergoing a style renaissance of sorts. For years, it was the unofficial uniform of off-duty professional athletes, finance bros, and your dad — a garment prized primarily for its comfort and functionality. But more recently, it’s been embraced as a fashion statement (at least according to the kids on TikTok). Case in point: The J.Crew Heritage Cotton Quarter-Zip Sweater, a revival of one of the brand’s popular ’90s cotton sweaters, still feels contemporary. It layers effortlessly — under a spring jacket or over a button-up or white T-shirt — without giving office vibes (though it would be totally fine in an office). It’s made from soft, high-quality cotton, and its sturdy collar actually holds its shape. The ribbed cuffs and hem add a touch of polish. This quarter-zip sweater is soft, breathable, and built for layering. The midweight, 100% cotton knit feels soft yet substantial against the skin. It provides a nice amount of warmth in a slim silhouette, and it looks equally good over a T-shirt or a button-down or under a light jacket. It’s also low-maintenance: According to the label, this sweater can be machine-washed (on cold) and machine-dried (on low). When I followed those directions, there was no notable shrinkage. “It fits like a glove.” That’s how one tester described this sweater. And the design and fit are broadly appealing: It has a classic silhouette, a high neck with a roughly 8-inch zipper, and ribbing at the cuffs and hem. “Quarter-zips in general give me a Peyton Manning vibe, but this one is a bit less performance-y,” said one tester, who is 5-foot-11 and tested it in a size M. The sweater comes in sizes XS to XXL and in several versatile colors, including Navy (which I tested), Dark Cherry, and Carbon gray. And we found it ran true to size: I’m 6-foot-3 and wore a size L, which fit perfectly. The collar actually stands up. This is a small but important detail, and it separates a well-made quarter-zip top from a mediocre one. Many collars in this category are flimsy (including the one on the other quarter-zip shirt we tested, the Polo Ralph Lauren Luxury Jersey Quarter-Zip Pullover), and they fold over when unzipped (which I think kills the look). I prefer a stiff collar that stands up and gives off a kind of popped-jacket-collar vibe. This sweater’s collar holds its shape whether it’s zipped up or not. (And the collar is handy in cooler temps: The higher you zip it, the warmer the sweater gets.) Flaws but not dealbreakers The cotton is a bit thick for warmer weather. That’s a good thing overall, but it also means the sweater probably won’t work well in the summer. Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXL - Materials: 100% cotton - Colors: 13 A simple cotton shirt for lots of bodies: J.Crew Classic Piqué Polo Shirt Top pick This no-frills shirt comes in three cuts, so it suits a wide range of heights and builds. (Oddly, it’s available in only three colors.) The piqué cotton fabric feels slightly stiff at first, but it softens over time. J.Crew’s Classic Piqué Polo Shirt isn’t trying to reinvent the wheel, and that’s a big part of its appeal. This medium-weight cotton shirt is a nod to those worn on tennis courts in the 1930s, with a subtle piqué texture and signature details that have made the polo a wardrobe staple for decades. It comes in three cuts, so people of different heights and builds can find one that works. This polo looks more expensive than it is, and it’s often on sale. This is an old-school, by-the-book polo shirt. The design is clean and classic, and the self-fabric ribbed collar is stiff enough to be worn up or down. The shirt has a two-button placket, set-in sleeves, and a small tennis tail, which works nicely tucked or untucked. (An extended hem on the back of the shirt, a tennis tail was originally designed to keep a shirt tucked in while the wearer was playing tennis.) There’s no logo to speak of (although you can monogram it for $10), and for the logo-averse, that’s an advantage over our other short-sleeve polo pick, Polo Ralph Lauren’s The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt. Depending on how you style this polo, it can skew preppy, sporty, or just put-together. “It’s very understated, but still looks nice,” one tester said. The Classic Piqué Polo is a great office-to-dinner shirt that works well with jeans, chinos, shorts, and pretty much anything else. The downside is the limited color selection: White, Navy, and Black. The shirt comes in three cuts, so it can suit different builds. It’s available in Classic, Slim, and Tall (in sizes XS to XXL), so it can work for a variety of body types. I tested the Classic fit in a size L. I’m 6-foot-3 and have an athletic build, and the shirt sat comfortably across my shoulders, with little room in the chest and a gentle taper through the torso (which I found flattering and non-clingy); the sleeves were snug without being restrictive. Another tester, who is 5-foot-11 and slender, tested the Classic fit in M (his usual size) and found the cut a tad too billowy: “A slim fit probably would have been a better profile,” he said. It looks more expensive than it is. The Classic Piqué Polo is made from cotton that’s U.S. Cotton Trust Protocol–certified (this certification tracks sustainability and supply chain). The piqué material’s waffle-like texture feels comfortably sturdy — the kind of fabric that should last a while and get softer with age. It’s not quite as soft as the Polo Ralph Lauren shirt, and it’s slightly thicker, but it’s typically about $40 cheaper. At the time of writing, J.Crew had it marked down to under $50; at that price, you could buy two colors for less than the cost of one Polo Ralph Lauren shirt. Flaws but not dealbreakers The color selection is limited. The options are White, Navy, and Black. Key specs - Sizes: Classic (XS to XXL), Slim (XS to XL), Tall (M to XXL) - Material: cotton piqué - Colors: three The king of polos: Polo Ralph Lauren The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt and Polo Ralph Lauren Mesh Long-Sleeve Polo Shirt Top pick Made from a subtly textured cotton mesh weave, this classic delivers on its designer pedigree: It’s stylish, breathable, and comfortable. It comes in over 50 colors and multiple fits (including Big & Tall). But it’s pricey, and the logo can be polarizing. Polo Ralph Lauren’s The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt and Mesh Long-Sleeve Polo Shirt have set the standard for polo shirts since the brand first introduced them, in 1972. “I finally understand why these are basically synonymous with the term polo,” one tester said. “It feels easily dressed-up or dressed-down, and a cut above the others I’ve worn.” The breathable cotton mesh material is cool and comfortable: It’s smoother, lighter, and less nubby than traditional piqué. The short-sleeve version is a warm-weather staple; the long-sleeve style offers that same breathable texture along with a little more coverage for cooler temps and casual layering. There’s a reason these shirts are considered the polo shirts. Although Ralph Lauren didn’t invent the polo shirt — that honor goes to René Lacoste — it has long been the standard-bearer. Ever since the debut of Polo Ralph Lauren shirts, more than 50 years ago, they have embodied a preppy, aspirational vibe, but not in a stuffy way: They’re intended to look casual and effortless, and they break in over time. The classic cotton mesh shirt — available with short or long sleeves — is familiar, versatile, and genuinely comfortable. The waffle-like weave creates tiny air pockets between the fabric and skin, so it’s more breathable than a jersey knit. It’s made from ring-spun combed cotton — a fine, smooth yarn without the scratchy fibers found in cheaper materials. These shirts come in tons of colors. The short-sleeve version is available in a whopping 54 colors, while the long-sleeve version comes in seven. And the colors strike different vibes. For example, the dark-gray Barclay Heather (with bright green logo) and the Polo Black (with red logo) connote casual office Fridays, whereas the White (with navy logo) and Baja Pink (with baby-blue logo) both bring pure summer vibes. I tested the Heritage Royal color, a vibrant royal blue with a red logo, and I liked it — until I went to a restaurant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and noticed the staff members were all wearing the shirts, in the same color, as a uniform. (Next time I’ll go for the more subdued Parchment Cream.) They also come in multiple fits. In standard sizes (XS to XXL), the short-sleeve Iconic Mesh Polo is available in three cuts: Classic, Custom Slim, and Slim. The Classic cut is the roomiest, providing a fuller body, lower armholes, and longer sleeves; the Custom Slim cut has a trimmer waist and sleeves, but it’s only slightly slimmer across the body; and the Slim cut is fitted through the chest, back, and waist, with biceps-hugging sleeves. The short-sleeve style also comes in Big & Tall sizes, from 2X Big to 5X Big and M Tall to 4L Tall. (The long-sleeve style has fewer options: It comes in Classic and Custom Slim fits only, in sizes XS to XXL.) I’m 6-foot-3, and I tested the shirt in the Classic fit in a size L. The fit was fairly comfortable, but in the future I may try an XL for a more relaxed look, since I prefer to wear roomier clothing in the summer. Another tester, who is 5-foot-11 and slender, tested the shirt in the Classic fit in his usual size, M, and said it fit perfectly. You can wear these shirts with almost anything. The shirts slot right into a spring/summer wardrobe: They go with jeans, chinos, shorts, and even some dress trousers. The tennis tail in back works equally well tucked or untucked. Flaws but not dealbreakers Some people may find the neckline too restrictive. This shirt has a two-button placket, which felt unusually high and tight on my neck, even when it was fully unbuttoned. I was the only tester who had this issue, though, and I couldn’t find similar complaints online, so it may come down to personal preference. (Our J.Crew Classic Piqué Polo Shirt pick also has a two-button placket, but that one didn’t bother me.) It’s not for the logo-averse. We’re not typically pro-logo either, but we gave this one a pass because it’s an embroidered polo player. Key specs - Sizes: XS to XXL, in Classic, Custom Slim, and Slim fits (The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt); XS to XXL, in Classic and Custom Slim fits (Mesh Long-Sleeve Polo Shirt); 2X to 5X and L Tall to 4L Tall (The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt in Big & Tall) - Material: 100% cotton - Colors: over 50 (The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt), 11 (Mesh Long-Sleeve Polo Shirt); 10 (The Iconic Mesh Polo Shirt in Big & Tall) Why you should trust us I am a writer covering style and accessories for Wirecutter. I’m the author of our guides to the best men’s suits, the best pants for the office (and beyond), and the best white T-shirts, among others. I’ve written about style and many other topics for publications including The New York Times Magazine, GQ, and Esquire. And I have an almost bank-breaking obsession with menswear. For this guide to the best men’s lightweight knits, sweaters, and polos, I did the following things: - I researched nearly 100 garments. - I enlisted two colleagues, with different body types and tastes, to do additional testing on the garments. - To immerse myself in the category, I spent a full day making the rounds to roughly a dozen stores in New York City — including Banana Republic, Buck Mason, J.Crew, and Uniqlo — and tried on various knitwear. Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of my editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. How we picked and tested For this guide, we focused on lightweight knits. These are the pieces that will see you through milder weather and the transitional seasons: winter to spring, spring to summer, and summer to fall. We excluded anything that was too bulky or warm, as well as items in categories that already have their own dedicated guides (such as sweatshirts and cashmere sweaters). In the end, we decided to focus on a variety of knits made from cotton, merino wool, and related blends.
