We tested lightweight sweaters in various styles — including crewnecks, quarter-necks, and polos — along with classic short- and long-sleeve polo shirts. We sought versatile workhorse items that could be dressed up or down — the kind you’d wear to go to the office, run errands, or meet a friend for dinner. After compiling a (huge) initial list, I chose 24 garments to test myself. After I’d identified the most promising styles, I recruited two colleagues to test nine of the finalists. (One tester is 5-foot-11 and wears a size M; the other is 5-foot-7 and also wears a size M.) Their detailed feedback helped to inform our picks. To assess how this knitwear would fare in the wild, I wore each contender for at least a day (and usually more), and I experimented with different outfit and shoe combinations. I washed and dried each piece according to the labels, checking for shrinkage or other changes post-laundering. (Personally, I’m a stickler for following care instructions. And I recommend that you do the same, so your clothing has a longer life.) During testing, I spent nearly four weeks in New Orleans in March. It proved to be an interesting testing ground for lightweight knits. The temperature swung from the low 40s (Fahrenheit) to the high 70s. I also spent many hours indoors in institutional AC, which required layering. And many of the garments recommended in this guide proved indispensable. We made our picks based on the following criteria: Style: We looked for versatile pieces that would have broad appeal across many tastes and preferences. We wanted to find sweaters and polos that felt both modern and timeless — and that wouldn’t go out of style anytime soon. Fit: We searched for garments that would accommodate a range of body types. And we gave bonus points to items that came in a range of sizes and fits. Fabric: Nobody wants to throw on a garment that feels rough and itchy or that doesn’t breathe when it gets warmer outside. We focused on polos made with comfortable, high-quality knit fabric — mostly cotton or merino wool — that didn’t need special pampering to launder and maintain. Quality and construction: We considered the craftsmanship of each garment, examining the construction and details (such as ribbed cuffs and hems). Value: We tested items ranging from $60 to $275. As always, we were on the hunt for pieces that are made to last and worth every dollar. Other lightweight men’s knits worth considering If you want a super-lightweight merino sweater: The Proper Cloth Easy Care Italian Merino Crewneck Sweater (sizes XS to XXL) is so lightweight that it can feel like wearing a long-sleeve T-shirt. It’s made from 100% merino wool from Italy that’s soft and low-maintenance. (You can machine-wash this sweater on cold and even tumble-dry it on low.) I loved the slim, athletic fit. But it’s a little too pricey for what it is, especially compared with our similar (and much less expensive) Banana Republic Merino Crew-Neck Sweater pick. If you’re seeking a classic spring/summer cotton cable-knit: The Polo Ralph Lauren Cable-Knit Cotton Sweater is the quintessential Ralph Lauren sweater, and that’s its main draw. (For some, though, this could be the main drawback.) The textured, dimensional cable-knit and the iconic logo embroidered on the chest are instantly recognizable. This sweater is also very comfortable; made from 100% cotton, it feels soft and light against the skin and is just the right weight for a breezy morning walk on the beach. This crewneck has a standard fit, so it’s neither too slim nor too baggy, with rib-knit cuffs and hem. (It comes in sizes XS to XXL, and it’s sometimes available in Big & Tall sizes.) Style-wise, it matches nicely with jeans, chinos, and other casual pants; if you want to lean into the preppy look, this top can be layered over an oxford shirt. If you’re looking for an outrageously comfortable quarter-zip option: The Polo Ralph Lauren Luxury Jersey Quarter-Zip Pullover (sizes XS to XXL) makes you look like you’re properly dressed in a nice, lightweight sweater, yet it has the feel of a Sunday sweatshirt. The cotton-blend fabric (a smooth, lightweight mix of 69% cotton, 29% viscose, and 2% nylon) is “exceptionally comfortable,” according to one tester. I found myself reaching for this shirt in the spring, when I wanted a comfy extra layer both indoors and outdoors. This quarter-zip comes in about a dozen appealing colors (though a bit more variety would be nice). But the collar is annoyingly limp — the thin fabric doesn’t have enough structure to stand upright, unless it’s fully zipped. And the price (around $135) seemed a little high, though select colors do go on sale. If you want to splurge on a luxe cotton crewneck: For an everyday treat, the Todd Snyder Beechwood Crewneck Sweater (sizes XS to XXL) is an amazingly soft, good-looking sweater. It’s made from a notably lightweight organic cotton yarn that, according to the brand, has been specially spun to help it stay airy and hold its shape. The sweater is more elevated than a basic cotton crewneck. And it has interesting details, including raglan sleeves (which give it a sporty look) and a half-cardigan stitch (this knitting technique is characterized by a ribbed structure that gives the garment subtle texture). But it comes in just one color, Bisque (an easily stainable shade), and the price (around $250) is pretty steep for a cotton sweater. The competition Cotton polo shirts I have fond memories of Lacoste polos from the 1990s and early 2000s, and I’m an avid seeker of the brand’s vintagewear. But I was disappointed with the (short-sleeve) Lacoste Men’s Classic Fit Original L.12.12 Polo and Lacoste Men’s Classic Fit Long Sleeve L.12.12 Polo. The cotton was stiff and thin, and the fit was boxy; these shirts just weren’t worth the price. We tested the Lululemon Evolution Short-Sleeve Polo Shirt, thinking it would be nice to have a sportier polo in the mix. This shirt may be great on the golf course, but we didn’t love the sweat-wicking synthetic fabric (85% polyester, 10% lyocell, 5% Lycra), and the fit was too slim. If you’re on a tighter budget, the Gap Pique Polo Shirt and Quince Organic Cotton Long Sleeve Pique Polo are two perfectly adequate options. But they couldn’t compete with our J.Crew and Polo Ralph Lauren cotton polo picks. The Gap shirt had a too-tight fit, while the Quince one was slightly itchy against the skin. Sweaters The Reigning Champ Lightweight Merino Harry Cardigan seemed a little cheap and thin. At the time of writing, the brand was updating this style (and stock is already running low). Because we’ve been impressed by some of this brand’s other offerings, we’re looking forward to checking out the new model. The Quince Organic Cotton-Silk Pique Crewneck Sweater was soft to the touch. But the weave was so loose that it seemed as if this one wouldn’t hold its shape for long. The Quince 100% Organic Cotton Ribbed Crewneck Sweater, meanwhile, is slightly heavier than we’d prefer for warmer months, and it didn’t feel as luxurious as the other cotton pieces we recommend. The Buck Mason Seafarer Cotton Rib Cardigan is made from 100% cotton, and we thought it felt great. The design is kind of bland, however, and this one didn’t seem worth the price (over $200). The Suitsupply Cotton Silk Crewneck was way too slim and short. On my 6-foot-3 frame, the sweater (in a size L) squeezed my chest and belly, and it landed above my belt line.
